query:
Please review, with sources, in-situ process monitoring for a small lab-built laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine used to screen aluminium alloys, and rank what to add first. The machine: 500 W single-mode CW Yb fibre laser at 1070 nm, SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (20 mm aperture, mirrors coated for 1064 nm, no camera port), f = 160 mm fused-silica f-theta lens, a 2 in. fused-silica chamber window with a replaceable cover slide, a sealed 280 x 190 x 120 mm aluminium chamber in argon at +5 to +20 mbar with a 2.5-3 m/s cross-flow, interchangeable heated build plates of 25, 50 and 75 mm diameter at up to 200 C, 30-60 um layers, ~75-96 um spot, scan speed up to ~1.1 m/s. Powders: AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, and crack-prone 6xxx, 7xxx and 2xxx alloys with and without grain refiners (Zr, Sc, TiB2), so detecting solidification (hot) cracking matters. Monitoring already planned: (a) a 12 MP layer camera looking through a lid viewport 33 degrees off vertical, about 26 um per pixel over the plate, imaging after each spread and after lasing with a low raking light; (b) a coaxial silicon photodiode picking off 520-985 nm melt-pool emission with a dichroic between the shutter and the galvo, sampled at >= 100 kHz. We want to record what happens in the chamber as fully as possible (high resolution, high frame rate, high magnification), with extensive synchronised metadata, and learn about powder spreading, the melt pool, and when cracking happens during solidification.

Questions:
1. Solidification cracking: which in-situ methods have actually detected hot cracking during LPBF (or laser welding or DED) of crack-prone alloys (Al 6xxx/7xxx/2xxx, Ni superalloys such as CM247LC or IN738LC, others)? For each: sensor type (structure-borne acoustic emission under the plate, airborne microphones, fibre Bragg gratings, thermography, pyrometry, optical imaging, synchrotron X-ray), frequency band or wavelengths, sensor placement, how detections were validated (CT, metallography, operando X-ray), and detection rates or false-alarm rates. When does the crack form relative to the melt pool passing (time and distance), and is it ever visible optically at the surface? Does acoustic emission still work through a heated plate with a ceramic thermal break and bolted or foil interfaces; what sensor temperature limits and waveguides are used?
2. Coaxial melt-pool sensing through a galvo: photodiodes versus two-colour pyrometers versus coaxial high-speed cameras. Which wavelength bands and bandwidths are used, how much do 1064 nm scanner mirror coatings and f-theta chromatic aberration limit coaxial imaging (resolution, field, focus shift), and how are they calibrated (blackbody, tungsten lamp, melting-point references)? What melt-pool temperatures and cooling rates have been measured for aluminium alloys in LPBF, and how reliable is two-colour pyrometry on aluminium given its low and changing emissivity?
3. Off-axis high-speed imaging of the melt pool and spatter in research LPBF testbeds (for example Imperial College/Hooper, LLNL, NIST AMMT, Sandia, MIT, EMPA, PSI): frame rates, exposure, magnification and working distance, long-distance microscopes, illumination lasers (for example Cavitar Cavilux) and filters, viewing angle, and how cameras are mounted and windows protected from metal condensate. What is the cheapest setup that still resolves melt-pool and spatter dynamics usefully?
4. Powder spreading and layer quality: what image resolution and lighting detect streaks, short feed, particle-scale defects and super-elevated edges; what in-situ height mapping (fringe projection, laser-line profilometry, low-coherence or inline coherent imaging, triangulation with the scanner's pilot laser) has measured actual layer thickness, and to what accuracy? Has anyone imaged the spreading itself (the powder heap ahead of the blade) at high speed inside an LPBF chamber?
5. Thermal imaging in a small chamber: NIR, SWIR and MWIR cameras, window materials (sapphire, CaF2, ZnSe, germanium), emissivity problems for aluminium, frame rates achievable, and what thermography has shown about cooling, heat accumulation and cracking.
6. Data and synchronisation: which signals to record (scan-controller position and laser gate, commanded and actual laser power, photodiode, acoustic, cameras, plate temperatures, O2, dew point, gas flow, recoater), how to put them on one clock with a SCANLAB RTC-class controller, typical data rates and storage per build, data standards or schemas used (for example NIST, ASTM/ISO), and documented cases where monitoring data misled.
7. Priorities: for a lab machine with a monitoring budget of roughly 20,000-40,000 USD, rank the additions by what they teach about spreading, melt pool and cracking per dollar, and name specific commercial instruments and their approximate prices where you can.

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation
        - NON_RANDOMIZED: Non-randomized allocation
        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment
        - PARALLEL: Parallel assignment
        - CROSSOVER: Crossover assignment
        - FACTORIAL: Factorial assignment
        - SEQUENTIAL: Sequential assignment

    ObservationalModel:
        - COHORT: Cohort
        - CASE_CONTROL: Case-Control
        - CASE_ONLY: Case-Only
        - CASE_CROSSOVER: Case-Crossover
        - ECOLOGIC_OR_COMMUNITY: Ecologic or Community
        - FAMILY_BASED: Family-Based
        - DEFINED_POPULATION: Defined Population
        - NATURAL_HISTORY: Natural History
        - OTHER: Other

    DesignMasking:
        - NONE: None (Open Label)
        - SINGLE: Single
        - DOUBLE: Double
        - TRIPLE: Triple
        - QUADRUPLE: Quadruple

    WhoMasked:
        - PARTICIPANT: Participant
        - CARE_PROVIDER: Care Provider
        - INVESTIGATOR: Investigator
        - OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR: Outcomes Assessor

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):

Use the tools to answer the question: Please review, with sources, in-situ process monitoring for a small lab-built laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine used to screen aluminium alloys, and rank what to add first. The machine: 500 W single-mode CW Yb fibre laser at 1070 nm, SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (20 mm aperture, mirrors coated for 1064 nm, no camera port), f = 160 mm fused-silica f-theta lens, a 2 in. fused-silica chamber window with a replaceable cover slide, a sealed 280 x 190 x 120 mm aluminium chamber in argon at +5 to +20 mbar with a 2.5-3 m/s cross-flow, interchangeable heated build plates of 25, 50 and 75 mm diameter at up to 200 C, 30-60 um layers, ~75-96 um spot, scan speed up to ~1.1 m/s. Powders: AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, and crack-prone 6xxx, 7xxx and 2xxx alloys with and without grain refiners (Zr, Sc, TiB2), so detecting solidification (hot) cracking matters. Monitoring already planned: (a) a 12 MP layer camera looking through a lid viewport 33 degrees off vertical, about 26 um per pixel over the plate, imaging after each spread and after lasing with a low raking light; (b) a coaxial silicon photodiode picking off 520-985 nm melt-pool emission with a dichroic between the shutter and the galvo, sampled at >= 100 kHz. We want to record what happens in the chamber as fully as possible (high resolution, high frame rate, high magnification), with extensive synchronised metadata, and learn about powder spreading, the melt pool, and when cracking happens during solidification.

Questions:
1. Solidification cracking: which in-situ methods have actually detected hot cracking during LPBF (or laser welding or DED) of crack-prone alloys (Al 6xxx/7xxx/2xxx, Ni superalloys such as CM247LC or IN738LC, others)? For each: sensor type (structure-borne acoustic emission under the plate, airborne microphones, fibre Bragg gratings, thermography, pyrometry, optical imaging, synchrotron X-ray), frequency band or wavelengths, sensor placement, how detections were validated (CT, metallography, operando X-ray), and detection rates or false-alarm rates. When does the crack form relative to the melt pool passing (time and distance), and is it ever visible optically at the surface? Does acoustic emission still work through a heated plate with a ceramic thermal break and bolted or foil interfaces; what sensor temperature limits and waveguides are used?
2. Coaxial melt-pool sensing through a galvo: photodiodes versus two-colour pyrometers versus coaxial high-speed cameras. Which wavelength bands and bandwidths are used, how much do 1064 nm scanner mirror coatings and f-theta chromatic aberration limit coaxial imaging (resolution, field, focus shift), and how are they calibrated (blackbody, tungsten lamp, melting-point references)? What melt-pool temperatures and cooling rates have been measured for aluminium alloys in LPBF, and how reliable is two-colour pyrometry on aluminium given its low and changing emissivity?
3. Off-axis high-speed imaging of the melt pool and spatter in research LPBF testbeds (for example Imperial College/Hooper, LLNL, NIST AMMT, Sandia, MIT, EMPA, PSI): frame rates, exposure, magnification and working distance, long-distance microscopes, illumination lasers (for example Cavitar Cavilux) and filters, viewing angle, and how cameras are mounted and windows protected from metal condensate. What is the cheapest setup that still resolves melt-pool and spatter dynamics usefully?
4. Powder spreading and layer quality: what image resolution and lighting detect streaks, short feed, particle-scale defects and super-elevated edges; what in-situ height mapping (fringe projection, laser-line profilometry, low-coherence or inline coherent imaging, triangulation with the scanner's pilot laser) has measured actual layer thickness, and to what accuracy? Has anyone imaged the spreading itself (the powder heap ahead of the blade) at high speed inside an LPBF chamber?
5. Thermal imaging in a small chamber: NIR, SWIR and MWIR cameras, window materials (sapphire, CaF2, ZnSe, germanium), emissivity problems for aluminium, frame rates achievable, and what thermography has shown about cooling, heat accumulation and cracking.
6. Data and synchronisation: which signals to record (scan-controller position and laser gate, commanded and actual laser power, photodiode, acoustic, cameras, plate temperatures, O2, dew point, gas flow, recoater), how to put them on one clock with a SCANLAB RTC-class controller, typical data rates and storage per build, data standards or schemas used (for example NIST, ASTM/ISO), and documented cases where monitoring data misled.
7. Priorities: for a lab machine with a monitoring budget of roughly 20,000-40,000 USD, rank the additions by what they teach about spreading, melt pool and cracking per dollar, and name specific commercial instruments and their approximate prices where you can.

ABSTRACT Growing demand for multi-material Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) faces process control and quality monitoring challenges, particularly in ensuring precise material composition. This study explores optical and acoustic emission signals during LPBF processes with multiple materials, addressing challenges in process control and ensuring accurate material composition. Experimental data from processing five powder compositions were collected using a custom-built monitoring system in a commercial LPBF machine. The research categorised signals from LPBF processing various compositions, enhancing prediction accuracy by combining optical with acoustic data and training convolutional neural networks using contrastive learning. Latent spaces of trained models using two contrastive loss functions, clustered acoustic and optical emissions based on similarities, aligning with five compositions. Contrastive learning and sensor fusion were found to be essential for monitoring LPBF processes involving multiple materials. This research advances the understanding of multi-material LPBF, highlighting sensor fusion strategies’ potential for improving quality control in additive manufacturing. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT

Abstract:
<jats:title>Mise en œuvre d'un alliage d'aluminium structural par fusion laser sur lit de poudres : étude des mécanismes de fissuration</jats:title>
                <jats:p xml:lang="fr">Dans cette thèse, une analyse de la sensibilité à la fissuration à chaud en fonction (i) des paramètres de premier ordre (puissance, vitesse) du procédé de fusion laser sur lit de poudres (L-PBF : Laser Powder Bed Fusion) et (ii) de la variation de la teneur en soluté (Si et Mg principalement) est présentée pour l'alliage d'aluminium à durcissement structural 6061 (Al-0.8Si-1.2Mg wt%). Le mécanisme de fissuration à chaud est identifié comme une fissuration par solidification sur la base d'observations expérimentales des microstructures. En accord avec des travaux antérieurs publiés sur d’autres familles d’alliages, les fissures se propagent aux joints de grains de fortes désorientations et sont préférentiellement situées au centre des bains de fusion. En utilisant le critère de Rappaz-Drezet-Gremaud (RDG criterion) combiné à des simulations thermiques utilisant le formalisme de Rosenthal, la localisation des fissures correspond aux régions des bains de fusion ou la sollicitation mécanique intergranulaire est la plus élevée lors de la solidification. Des cartes de sensibilité à la fissuration à chaud sont ensuite développées pour prédire de manière simple les variations de sensibilité à la fissuration à chaud en fonction des paramètres du procédé de premier ordre, à savoir la puissance laser et la vitesse de balayage ainsi que des conditions de préchauffage. Les tendances prédites sont qualitativement en accord avec les observations expérimentales. Les résultats permettent de discuter de l'impact des conditions d’élaboration sur la réduction de la fissuration à chaud et également d’identifier les paramètres métallurgiques clés de ce mécanisme de fissuration.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Online quality control of advanced manufacturing processes often utilize process monitoring as a qualification method to reduce or eliminate time consuming and costly destructive and non-destructive tests. The need for process monitoring based qualification becomes more apparent with the advent of laser based additive manufacturing for complex geometries and lot-size-one production. However, the usability of the process monitoring solution heavily relies on the accuracy of the established alignment and assignment of process signals to specific part and defects herein. This research proposes a data fusion strategy for data pre-processing to structure and align multi-source sensor data for improving correlation accuracy in process monitoring. A laser powder bed fusion system equipped with a photodiode-based co-axial melt pool monitoring is used for the study. First, the monitoring system collects photon emission data from the melt pool using photodiodes with high frequency (>100 kHz) which are aligned spatially and temporally using position data (xy-coordinates) of the galvanometer scanner and the laser ON/OFF signals. Next, a clustering approach is used to assign each photodiode signal with the individual parts on the build platform. Finally, correlation between melt pool monitoring signals and part level porosity is studied using micro-computed X-ray tomography (μCT) from a build job containing parts produced under varying process conditions.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Reliable process monitoring is critical for advancing laser powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), as it provides the process information required for corrective control actions to prevent defects such as lack-of-fusion and keyhole porosity. A promising approach for PBF-LB/M process monitoring is coaxial measurement of light emitted from the meltpool area. More than two hundred research studies on coaxial monitoring of the meltpool have been performed, but there is still no validated and reliable method for measuring a suitable variable that could be directly used as an input for high-resolution control of the PBF-LB/M process, enabling process parameters such as laser power and scan speed to be dynamically adjusted not only at the part level, but locally for individual micrometer-scale segments along the scan track. This work reviews existing research studies on coaxial meltpool monitoring and identifies potential future research and development directions toward a standard and reliable meltpool monitoring method. Meltpool depth is identified as a particularly promising control-relevant variable. With the ability to monitor and control meltpool depth, it is possible to avoid undesirable process conditions due to too high or too low energy input, which would result in defects like keyhole porosity or lack-of-fusion. However, only five studies have attempted to estimate the melt pool depth coaxially during the PBF-LB/M process. Despite these attempts, there is no sufficiently validated method for high-resolution coaxial monitoring of meltpool depth in PBF-LB/M. The potential solution seems to be in combining concepts and recent discoveries from two-color coaxial camera- and photodiode-based meltpool area monitoring approaches. Based on the existing literature and hands-on experiences with establishing and working with coaxial monitoring systems, this work also provides guidelines and lists the most common challenges for implementing coaxial monitoring of the meltpool in the PBF-LB/M process.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is a key technology for high-precision manufacturing of complex-shaped metallic components. A detailed understanding of the spatter and melt pool behavior during the process is essential for optimizing the process parameters and improving the part quality. This study presents an observation system that combines ultrahigh-speed imaging at 1,000,000 frames per second (fps) with quad-directional (four-direction) laser illumination. This setup facilitates real-time, high-fidelity visualization of dynamic phenomena such as melt pool evolution and spatter generation, which are difficult to observe using conventional single-direction illumination, by reducing self-shadowing and clarifying feature contours. Using this system, transient melt pool behavior with and without spatter was contrasted across four laser powers of 50, 100, 150, and 200 W and four scanning speeds of 50, 100, 150, and 200 mm/s; under spatter-generating conditions, surface protrusions grew more rapidly and detached as spatter once their velocity and geometry were sufficient to overcome surface tension, whereas under nonspattering conditions, they were reabsorbed before detachment. Image analysis quantified frame-to-frame brightness fluctuations on the melt pool surface as a relative indicator of dynamic surface instability and revealed its dependence on process parameters, particularly the volumetric energy density. The results support a mechanism in which dynamic surface instability promotes spatter formation. This approach provides a powerful tool for in-situ analysis of LPBF and contributes to the development of advanced process control and quality assurance in metal additive manufacturing, including real-time spatter control and process-window optimization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conceptual Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Quad-directional illumination paired with an ultrahigh-speed camera capturing one million frames per second makes rapid changes on the melt pool surface during laser powder bed fusion clearly observable. A simple measure of surface-brightness fluctuation summarizes the degree of surface instability and links it to the energy input per unit volume. When surface bumps grow quickly and maintain a favorable shape, they detach as spatter; under calmer settings they are reabsorbed. These insights help select more stable process windows and refine scan strategies to reduce spatter in metal additive manufacturing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Abstract:
<jats:p>While the majority of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) metal additive manufacturing uses a continuous wave (CW) laser heat source, some commercial applications of LPBF additive manufacturing instead involve the modulation of the laser power on tens-of-microsecond timescales as an adjustable process variable. This article reports the use of in situ, high speed x-ray and optical imaging to probe melt pool fluid flow, defect formation, and nearby powder motion during LPBF with both modulated and CW laser heat sources. We observe melt pool dynamics unique to modulated laser melting even at very high duty cycles that are related to fluctuations in vapor depression depth, complex pore formation mechanisms, and changes to denudation physics when compared to CW melting. These behaviors are present in Ti–6Al–4V, 316L stainless steel, and AL1100 alloys but vary slightly as a function of material, indicating a substantial dependence on the viscosity and surface tension of the liquid metal. While high duty cycles produce weld tracks of comparable quality to CW melting, lower duty cycles introduce substantial defect concentrations. At intermediate duty cycles, careful control of modulation parameters can repeatably and precisely yield one pore per laser pulse, suggesting a method for intentionally inserting engineered porosity at specific sites during an LPBF build.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The production of reliable turbo machinery, particularly gas turbine blades, is a major global challenge. This capability serves as a key indicator of a nation’s industrial base, technological prowess, and comprehensive strength. Critical components in aircraft engines and gas turbines operate under extreme conditions, including high temperatures, high pressures, and substantial mechanical stresses. Consequently, there is a growing urgency to develop cost-effective and time-efficient repair strategies to enhance engine performance and efficiency. However, many mission-critical parts, especially high-pressure (HP) blades, are prone to severe damage. Moreover, taking equipment offline for blade maintenance and repair is a time-consuming process. It is also highly costly to restore these essential components to full functionality. Since 1996, researchers have focused on applying laser metal deposition (LMD) additive manufacturing technology for high-performance repair and remanufacturing of aerospace engines and industrial gas turbine (IGT) blades. Empirical studies have demonstrated that depositing a high-quality, erosion-resistant protective coating on the leading edge of HP blades effectively extends the service life of turbine blades in both aircraft engines and industrial gas turbines. This study systematically outlines the technical workflow of the proposed methodology and provides a concise perspective on emerging development trends.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Metal additive manufacturing (AM) facilitates the production of geometrically complex components, yet its broader industrial use remains limited by the risk of defect formation and uncertainties in their detection, originating from the highly dynamic and high-temperature process environment. To make additive manufacturing more reliable and establish high-quality parts, it is important to understand how these defects form and how their characteristics appear during the process. This review explains the main causes of common defects, such as cracking, porosity, lack of fusion, and inclusions in metal AM processes, including Powder Bed Fusion and Directed Energy Deposition. It also connects main defect formation mechanisms to the optical, thermal, acoustic, and spectroscopic signals that can be measured during the process. Moreover, it is described how commonly used in situ monitoring systems work and how their signals correspond to melt pool dynamics, vapor plume, particle movement, and the solidification process for each kind of defect. An overview is provided of how data from these systems are analyzed, including the extraction of features from images, the evaluation of temperature fields, and the use of time and frequency domain techniques for various signals. By linking the physics of defect formation to measurable process signals, the interpretation of sensor data is enabled, and potential strategies for monitoring specific problems are outlined. Finally, recent developments are examined, including the integration of multiple sensors, advanced feature-representation approaches, and real-time data interpretation coupled with adaptive control. Together, these directions represent promising advances towards more intelligent and reliable monitoring systems for the future of metal AM.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Welding inspection is a critical process that can be severely time-consuming, resulting in productivity delays, especially when destructive or invasive processes are required. This paper defines the novel approach to investigate the physical correlation between common imperfections found in arc welding and the propensity to determine these through the identification of signatures using acoustic emission sensors. Through a set of experiments engineered to induce prominent imperfections (cracks and other anomalies) using a popular welding process and the use of AE technology (both airborne and contact), it provides confirmation that the verification of physical anomalies can indeed be identified through variations in obtained noise frequency signatures. This in situ information provides signals during and after solidification to inform operators of the deposit/HAZ integrity to support the advanced warning of unwanted anomalies and of whether the weld/fabrication process should be halted to undertake rework before completing the fabrication. Experimentation was carried out based on an acceptable set of parameters where extracted data from the sensors were recorded, analysed, and compared with the resultant microstructure. This may allow signal phenomena to be captured and catalogued for future use in referencing against known anomalies.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Powder Bed Fusion – Laser Beam (PBF–LB) of Ni-base superalloys is highly attractive for components in high temperatures applications, particularly within the aerospace and industrial gas turbine sectors. This interest is due to the high degree of design freedom which allows complex internal cooling channels that significantly improve the component lifetime or enable higher operating temperatures, thereby boosting gas turbine efficiency. However, superalloys containing high volume fraction of γ′, like CM247LC with 60 to 70 vol.%, exhibit poor PBF–LB processibility, suffering from both micro- and macro-cracking, and have poor and anisotropic creep performance. The aim of the thesis is to understand the impact of the intricate relationships between PBF–LB process parameters, cracking, residual stresses, heat treatment, microstructure and creep performance. Using operando synchrotron X-ray radiography, the observed micro-cracking is confirmed to occur during solidification. The micro-cracks are observed at the high angle grain boundaries exhibiting a distinct solidification structure consistent with the solidification cracking mechanism. Solidification cracking is mitigated either through alloy/powder modification or through process parameter optimization with any remnant solidification cracks eliminated through hot isostatic pressing (HIP). However, the presence of macro-cracks, particularly around stress concentrators, is observed after HIP. This macro-cracking is identified as strain age cracking (SAC) due to the γ′ precipitation. SAC is minimized by a tailored HIP using higher pressure before reaching solution treatment temperature. Minimizing residual stress by varying PBF–LB process parameters, including scan strategies, is effective in minimizing SAC. The solution heat treatment developed for cast CM247LC when applied to CM247LC produced via PBF–LB indicated limited grain growth and poor creep performance. A re-designed HIP combined with a solution heat treatment at higher temperature of 1280 °C demonstrates 23% increase in creep rupture life compared to the standard 1250 °C, yielding slightly coarser grains, improved grain boundary decoration, and finer uniform cuboidal γ′ precipitates. Despite this optimization, the creep performance remained inferior to that of the cast alloy. Subsequent tailoring of the PBF–LB process to produce a highly columnar and anisotropic microstructure significantly increased the creep life along the build direction. In summary, this investigation into the PBF–LB of CM247LC demonstrates that the effective mitigation of cracking and improvement of creep performance requires tailored PBF–LB processing and post-processing heat treatment strategies.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) has revolutionized production across industries, yet persistent challenges in defect detection and process reliability necessitate advanced in situ monitoring solutions. While non-destructive evaluation (NDE) techniques such as X-ray computed tomography, thermography, and ultrasonic testing have been widely adopted, the critical role of 3D surface topographic monitoring remains underutilized for real-time anomaly detection. This work comprehensively reviews the 3D surface monitoring of AM processes, such as Laser powder bed fusion, directed energy deposition, material extrusion, and material jetting, highlighting the current state and challenges. Furthermore, the article discusses the state-of-the-art advancements in closed-loop feedback control systems, sensor fusion, and machine learning algorithms to integrate 3D surface data with various process signatures to dynamically adjust laser parameters and scan strategies. Guidance has been provided on the best 3D monitoring technique for each of the AM processes. Motivated by manufacturing labor shortages, the high skill required to operate and troubleshoot some of these additive manufacturing techniques, and zero-defect manufacturing goals, this paper also explores the metamorphosis towards autonomous AM systems and adaptive process optimization and explores the role and importance of real-time 3D monitoring in that transition.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is highly susceptible to process instabilities, and defects generated during fabrication are often irreversible. Although Fringe Projection Profilometry (FPP) has emerged as a cost-effective, non-contact technique for surface metrology in LPBF, existing implementations are largely limited to post-layer inspection and cannot capture the transient surface evolution during active laser processing. In this study, a single-view FPP system was designed, assembled, and integrated into a commercial LPBF machine to enable continuous, time-resolved, in situ 4D (x, y, z, time) monitoring throughout the printing process. The proposed system continuously measures both the freshly spread powder bed and the evolving build surface during contour and infill scanning. Experimental results demonstrate the capability to reconstruct the dynamic evolution of the build surface throughout an entire manufacturing cycle, including powder spreading, contour scanning, infill formation, and layer completion. Furthermore, by registering the reconstructed surfaces of successive layers within a common coordinate system, the layer-by-layer material accumulation process can be digitally visualized and quantified. The proposed approach establishes a time-resolved, in situ 4D surface metrology framework for LPBF and provides a new experimental capability for investigating short-term post-scan surface evolution during additive manufacturing.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) holds promise to efficiently produce metal parts. However, LPBF incurs stochastic melt pool (MP) spattering, which would roughen workpiece in-process surface, thus weakening inter-layer bonding and causing issues like porosity, powder contamination, and recoater intervention. Understanding the consequential effect of MP spattering on layer surface remains difficult due to the lack of process monitoring capability for concurrently tracking MP spatters and characterizing layer surfaces. In this work, using our lab-designed LPBF-specific fringe projection profilometry and an off-axis camera, we quantify the correlation between MP spattering and in-process layer surface roughness for the first time to reveal the influence of MP spatters on process anomaly and part defects. A method of extracting and registering MP spattering metrics is developed by machine learning of the in-situ imaging data. Each image is analyzed to obtain the MP center location and the spatter count and ejection angle. These MP spatter signatures are registered for each monitored MP across each layer. Regression modeling is used to correlate registered MP spatter signature and its processing parameters with layer surface topography measured by the in-situ FPP. We find that the attained MP spatter feature profile can help predict the layer surface roughness more accurately (>50% less error), in contrast to the conventional approaches that would only use nominal process setting. This is because the spatter information can reflect key process changes including the deviations in actual laser scan parameters and their effects. The results corroborate the importance of spatter monitoring and the distinct influence of spattering on layer surface roughness. Our work paves a foundation to thoroughly elucidate and effectively control the role of MP spattering in defect formation during LPBF.

Abstract:
ABSTRACT Additive manufacturing offers a range of novel applications. However, the manufacturing process is complex and the production of almost defect-free parts with high reliability and durability is still a challenge. Thermography is a valuable tool for process surveillance, especially in metal additive manufacturing processes. The high process temperatures allow one to use cameras usually operating in the visible spectral range. Here, we compare the results of measurements during the manufacturing process of a commercial laser metal deposition setup using a mid wavelength infrared camera with those from a short wavelength infrared camera and those from a visual spectrum high-speed camera with band pass filter in the near infrared range.

Abstract:
Over the past decade, significant research has focused on detecting abnormalities in metal laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) additive manufacturing. Effective online monitoring systems are crucial for enhancing process stability, repeatability, and the quality of final components. Therefore, the development of in situ detection mechanisms has become essential for metal L-PBF systems, making efficient closed-loop control strategies to adjust process parameters in real time vital. This paper presents an overview of current in situ monitoring systems used in metal L-PBF, complemented by ex situ characterizations. It discusses in situ techniques employed in L-PBF and evaluates the applicability of commercial systems. The review covers optical, thermal, acoustic, and X-ray in situ methods, along with destructive and non-destructive ex situ methods like optical, Archimedes, and X-ray characterization techniques. Each technique is analyzed based on the sensor used for defect detection and the type or size of defects. Optical in situ monitoring primarily identifies large defects from powder bed abnormalities, while thermal methods detect defects as small as 100 µm and keyholes. Thermal in situ detection techniques are notable for their applicability to commercial devices and efficacy in detecting subsurface defects. Computed tomography scanning excels in locating porosity in 3D space with high accuracy. This study also explores the advantages of multi-sensor in situ techniques, such as combining optical and thermal sensors, and concludes by addressing current research needs and potential applications of multi-sensor systems.

Abstract:
The main aim of the study was to analyse the strain rate sensitivity of the compressive deformation response in bulk 3D-printed samples from 316L stainless steel according to the printing orientation. The laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) method of metal additive manufacturing was utilised for the production of the samples with three different printing orientations: 0∘, 45∘, and 90∘. The specimens were experimentally investigated during uni-axial quasi-static and dynamic loading. A split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) apparatus was used for the dynamic experiments. The experiments were observed using a high-resolution (quasi-static loading) or a high-speed visible-light camera and a high-speed thermographic camera (dynamic loading) to allow for the quantitative and qualitative analysis of the deformation processes. Digital image correlation (DIC) software was used for the evaluation of displacement fields. To assess the deformation behaviour of the 3D-printed bulk samples and strain rate related properties, an analysis of the true stress–true strain diagrams from quasi-static and dynamic experiments as well as the thermograms captured during the dynamic loading was performed. The results revealed a strong strain rate effect on the mechanical response of the investigated material. Furthermore, a dependency of the strain-rate sensitivity on the printing orientation was identified.

Abstract:

                  <jats:p>Significant advances have been made in the field of Additive Manufacturing (AM) across various manufacturing processes. Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is one of the most widely adopted metal AM processes in the industry, which employs energy sources such as lasers to melt powder materials. While the LPBF process offers numerous advantages, such as the ability to produce complex geometries and multiple parts simultaneously, it also presents challenges in the form of defects such as porosity, residual stresses, and cracks that need to be addressed. Conducting experiments to identify and eliminate these defects can be prohibitively expensive, motivating the development of alternative predictive approaches. Numerical modeling and simulation techniques provide a cost-effective alternative to experimental approaches, enabling analyses ranging from thermal histories and microstructural evolution to mechanical property prediction and defect identification in fabricated components. In recent years, Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms have emerged as viable alternative tools to accelerate process understanding, defect prediction, and parameter optimization. This review provides a comprehensive overview of ML-based approaches applied to LPBF, emphasizing the importance of understanding the underlying physical phenomena that significantly influence data collection, preprocessing, and feature engineering strategies essential for effective model training and validation. It offers a structured framework for researchers seeking to leverage ML methods to enhance predictive accuracy and computational efficiency, particularly through simulation-driven data generation for model development.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Direct laser metal deposition (LMD–DED) is an additive manufacturing (AM) process that is used to build up and repair high-quality metal components. It works by overlapping layers of powder material and melting them with a laser. To get a stable process without defects and to reach, at the same time, high mechanical properties, a robust assessment and control of the process parameters, and above all of their combination, is required. The ideal goal is to assure the online control, to stop or correct the process in case of unexpected anomalies. In this work, a robust online monitoring of the laser metal deposition (LMD–DED) process based on the use of infrared thermography was developed and proposed. After choosing the suitable process parameters, a customized design of experiments (DOE) was set, and the statistical analysis of different thermal features was carried out to develop the most robust models that correlate them with the input process parameters (laser power, scanning speed, and powder flow rate). The proposed procedure was based on the extraction of different thermal features from suited regions of interest (ROI), performing statistical analyses by means of analysis of variance (ANOVA) and building regression models to correlate the process parameters with the thermal behavior. The obtained results demonstrated the possibility to control the process by means of the chosen thermal features, independent of the position of the ROI. Moreover, the possibility to use the models to detect typical AM defects, and anomalies, online directly during the process, has been proved and verified by destructive macrographs carried out on the manufactured coupons.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is an additive manufacturing (AM) technique with growing industrial applications. Variations in laser power, scan speed, and thermal conditions can lead to defects such as porosity, cracks, and deformations. Effective Real-time monitoring and control in LPBF are crucial for ensuring process stability, defect mitigation, and part quality consistency as well as improving production efficiency. Existing LPBF process monitoring and control research often focuses on the performance of the algorithms, such as prediction accuracy and decision-making optimization without addressing real-time implementability and discussing the trade-offs between algorithm complexity and computation feasibility. Evaluation of computational resources is essential for advanced monitoring and control algorithm implementation. For real-time data processing and control, Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) is an ideal computing platform for sub millisecond applications. In LPBF AM, melt pool image (MPI)-based process monitoring with machine learning has been widely studied for part quality prediction and control. This paper conducts computing performance evaluation for FPGA implementation of real-time MPI-based LPBF process monitoring. More specifically, latency and resource utilization are analyzed for various advanced analytical algorithms. Two case studies illustrate this evaluation: (1) High-Level Synthesis (HLS)-based analysis of MP feature extraction and (2) High-Level Synthesis for Machine Learning (HLS4ML)-based evaluation of neural network inference for anomaly detection. These cases demonstrate the applicability of FPGA-based solutions to in-process advanced data analytics during LPBF, providing insights for researchers and engineers to develop scalable and efficient real-time control systems for LPBF.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion exhibits many advantages for manufacturing complex geometries from hard to machine alloys such as IN625. However, a major drawback is the formation of high tensile residual stresses, and the complex relationship between the process parameters and the residual stresses has not been fully investigated. The current study presents multi-scale models to examine the variation of process parameters on melt pool dimensions, cyclic temperature evolutions, cooling rate, and cyclic stress generation and how they affect the stress end state. In addition, the effect of the same energy density, which is often overlooked, on the generated residual stresses is investigated. Multi-level validation is performed based on melt pool dimensions, temperature measurements with a two-color pyrometer, and finally, in-depth residual stress measurement. The results show that scan speed has the strongest effect on residual stresses, followed by laser power and hatch spacing. The results are explained in light of the non-linear temperature evolution, temperature gradient, and cooling rate during laser exposure, cooling time, and the rate during recoating time.

Abstract:
This study aims to measure the cooling rates or, more precisely, the cooling durations of single laser tracks by pyrometry within the laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) process. Two-color, as well as one-color pyrometers are tested within this work. Regarding the second, the emissivity of the investigated 30CrMoNb5-2 alloy is determined in-situ within the L-PBF system in order to measure temperature instead of arbitrary units. This is done by heating up printed samples and verifying the measured pyrometer signal by comparing it to values obtained by thermocouples attached to the samples. In addition, the precision of two-color pyrometry is verified for the given setup. Following the verification experiments, single laser track experiments are conducted. The obtained signals prove to be partially distorted mainly due to by-products such as smoke and weld beads arising from the melt pool. To encounter this problem, a new fitting method is presented and experimentally validated. Melt pools resulting from different cooling durations are analyzed by EBSD. These measurements show areas of extreme deformation or potential amorphization correlating with the cooling durations. The obtained cooling duration can be used for the validation of simulations as well as for the correlation of corresponding microstructure and process parameters.

From text 'fardan2026unveilingcrackmitigation pages 1-2'.

Ahmed Fardan, Gowtham Soundarapandiyan, Vigneashwara Pandiyan, Steven Van Petegem, Efthymios Polatidis, Sofia Kazi, Sneha Goel, Camille Pauzon, Federica Marone, Bharat Mehta, Annapaola Parrilli, Håkan Brodin, and Eduard Hryha. Unveiling crack mitigation pathways in powder bed fusion–laser beam of cm247lc: an operando x-ray radiography study of hf and nano-y2o3 additions. Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 11:9831-9849, Aug 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-026-01876-5, doi:10.1007/s40964-026-01876-5. This article has 1 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies two in-situ methods used to detect hot cracking during PBF-LB of crack-prone CM247LC: operando synchrotron X-ray radiography and bulk acoustic emission (AE). Synchrotron radiography provides direct, real-time visualization of crack formation and was synchronized with AE in this study. AE sensors detect transient elastic waves propagating through the solid material or build substrate following rapid stress redistribution; relevant events include crack initiation, crack propagation, thermal contraction, phase transformation, and dislocation motion. The excerpt states that AE interpretation can use amplitude, frequency content, and event timing, but it does not provide numerical frequency bands or detailed sensor geometry beyond placement on/through the solid material or build substrate. The radiography studies distinguish cracking during processing and have observed simultaneous solidification and liquation cracks. Solidification cracking occurs near the end of melt-pool solidification, when tensile stresses separate solute-rich interdendritic liquid. The excerpt does not discuss thermography or optical sensing, nor does it report specific validation procedures such as metallographic sectioning or tomography; it emphasizes operando observation as overcoming limitations of post-mortem microscopy.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'nobari2026mechanismssensorsand pages 9-11'.

Sanae Tajalli Nobari, Fabian Hanning, Yongcui Mi, and Joerg Volpp. Mechanisms, sensors, and signals for defect formation and in situ monitoring in metal additive manufacturing. Eng, 7:129, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/eng7030129, doi:10.3390/eng7030129. This article has 7 citations.

The excerpt describes in-situ acoustic emission (AE) and thermal sensing for detecting cracking in metal additive manufacturing, with a specific example from DED-LB/M of SiC-particle-reinforced 316L composites. AE sensors detect elastic waves released by sudden stress relaxation during crack initiation, delamination, or related events; piezoelectric sensors receive waves propagating through the substrate or deposited layers. Hot-cracking emissions are summarized as spanning approximately 100–700 kHz, with peak frequencies around 300–600 kHz, while rapid initiation is associated with bursts at 300–600 kHz and above. Lower frequencies are linked to slower crack growth or process instabilities. In the cited DED example, microcracking during rapid cooling generated a distinctive 12–16 kHz audible signal; high-pass filtering and HPSS separated it from process noise. Validation used optical microscopy, which found voids and surface defects in cracked samples and smooth surfaces in crack-free samples, together with spectrogram comparison. Thermal sensing is presented as recording temperature changes before or during crack formation, but no specific thermography configuration is given. The excerpt does not provide synchrotron X-ray results, detailed optical-sensor placement, exact AE sensor locations, or a definitive timing relationship between hot-crack formation and the melt pool; it only relates cracking to rapid cooling and stress release during or after processing.

From text 'lafirenza2025developmentofinsitu pages 44-46'.

M Lafirenza. Development of in-situ optical sensor-based monitoring methodologies for additive manufacturing processes. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt identifies acoustic-emission (AE) monitoring as the clearest method for detecting cracking in L-DED. AE signals are associated with cracking, pore formation, deformation, and machine-state events. Both contact sensors and contactless sensors were used: contact sensors were mounted on the substrate or uppermost part of the deposited component, while contactless implementations used a laser vibrometer and an optical microphone. The latter detected layer cracking caused by thermal stress and heat-affected-zone cracking, and crack analysis was validated using normalized acoustic-energy images. Other validation approaches included correlating acoustic features with crack location and using amplitude and duration parameters for crack-extension monitoring; machine-learning methods, including K-means clustering, distinguished pore- and crack-generated signals. The excerpt also reports optical plasma methods, particularly LIBS, identifying cracks and pores in real time through spectral-intensity differences, although it does not specify sensor placement, frequency bands, or whether the cracks were solidification-hot cracks. Synchrotron X-ray methods captured melt-pool morphology, internal defects, powder sintering, pore formation, and solidification kinetics, but no explicit crack-detection result is given. No frequency ranges or precise crack timing relative to the melt pool are provided; the AE discussion links cracking to thermal stress, cooling, and deposition events rather than stating an exact temporal position.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2023.103579, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2023.103579. This article has 34 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides evidence for in-situ detection of cracking during DED of the crack-prone nickel superalloy CM247LC, using optical inline coherent imaging (ICI), synchrotron X-ray imaging, and, in prior work, acoustic emission (AE). ICI monitored surface topology and detected crack openings as small as 7 µm, including subsurface signal. The system was positioned off-axis at 24° relative to the laser, allowing integration without modifying laser-delivery optics. Its measurements were registered to the laser position with <10 µm lateral and <3 µm depth accuracy. Synchrotron radiographs were used to observe subsurface crack healing and growth, while radiographs validated the ICI topology measurements with a correlation greater than 0.93. Cracks were intentionally induced in surface valleys associated with humping. The excerpt mentions AE as the only previously reported DED method that correlated monitoring with cracking, but gives no AE frequency bands, sensor placement, or detailed validation protocol. It also does not specify the exact timing of crack formation relative to the melt pool or establish whether the observed cracking is definitively hot/solidification cracking. No thermography results, LPBF examples, or laser-welding examples are included in this excerpt.

From text 'lafirenza2025developmentofinsitu pages 46-49'.

M Lafirenza. Development of in-situ optical sensor-based monitoring methodologies for additive manufacturing processes. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt provides relevant evidence mainly for in-situ crack monitoring in L-DED, but it does not specifically identify solidification (hot) cracking, LPBF, laser welding, acoustic-emission frequency bands, sensor placement, synchrotron X-ray methods, or the precise timing of crack formation relative to the melt pool. Acoustic emission (AE) was used to monitor layer cracking associated with thermal stress and HAZ cracking, and to monitor crack extension by relating AE amplitude and duration to crack location. In mixed-metal powder deposition, machine-learning methods, including K-Means clustering, distinguished pore-generated from crack-generated signals. A deep-learning SRCD model detected crack defects with 99.76% accuracy, while t-SNE-based time/frequency-domain processing achieved over 89% classification accuracy under different process parameters. AE is therefore presented as useful for real-time defect diagnosis, although weak signals, environmental noise, and high-temperature limitations complicate acquisition; contact sensors may require cooling. Thermal monitoring used contactless pyrometers and infrared cameras to capture melt-pool temperature and cooling behavior, but the excerpt does not report direct detection or temporal localization of hot cracks. Thermal methods are also limited by emissivity, reflections, plasma, and powder-flash interference. No synchrotron X-ray evidence is included.
