AE was used to detect layer delamination and HAZ cracking; acoustic-energy peaks distinguished cracking mechanisms, while crack-free samples had a background AE energy of approximately 0.03. STFT and CWT were applied to AE signals: both detected transient events, but STFT required less computational effort, whereas CWT offered greater resolution. Another AE system used PCA and unsupervised K-means clustering, with signal energy being the most important classification feature; cracking produced short-duration, high-amplitude, high-energy signals. Validation included optical microscopy (OM), liquid-penetrant inspection, microscopic analysis, and comparison with conventional inspections. Thermal monitoring measured melt-pool temperature fields, temperature evolution, gradients, melt-pool size and shape, and cooling behavior. Cracks were associated with elevated temperatures, high thermal gradients, excessive thermal fluctuations, and temperature changes when the laser passed over simulated cracking. Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The metal additive manufacturing industry has experienced significant advancement and growth over the past decades. Powder bed fusion stands out as a promising technology for industries such as aerospace and biomedical due to its ability to produce complex geometries with short lead times. A critical drawback of the technology is the potential for defects to arise, restricting full adoption by these highly regulated industries. Achieving process control remains challenging due to many interacting process variables, coupled with stochastic deviations which can result in defects. While these defects may be detected using ex-situ techniques, this is usually a very costly step. Hence, a critical challenge is the need for in-situ detection of defects to improve quality assurance. Despite the variety of in-situ sensors and defect detection algorithms that are emerging in commercial machines, detection accuracy and efficacy remain problematic. These sensors generate large, complex datasets that traditional pattern detection methods struggle to interpret. This presents an excellent opportunity for machine learning, which can uncover complex patterns in large volumes of multi-modal data. This paper offers a critical review of the current state-of-the-art with respect to in-situ monitoring of the powder bed fusion process. It includes a general overview of the various defect types, as well as analysis of different sensing techniques. Special emphasis is placed on the types of machine learning models employed and the methods used to generate their training data. Key breakthroughs are highlighted, and actionable recommendations are provided for future research and areas of improvement.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Metal powder bed fusion (PBF) is an advanced metal additive manufacturing (AM) technology. Compared with traditional manufacturing techniques, PBF has a higher degree of design freedom. Currently, although PBF has received extensive attention in fields with high–quality standards such as aerospace and automotive, there are some disadvantages, namely poor process quality and insufficient stability, which make it difficult to apply the technology to the manufacture of critical components. In order to surmount these limitations, it is necessary to monitor the process. Online monitoring technology can detect defects in time and provide certain feedback control, so it can greatly enhance the stability of the process, thereby ensuring its quality of the process. This paper presents the current status of online monitoring technology of the metal PBF process from the aspects of powder recoating monitoring, powder bed inspection, building process monitoring, and melt layer detection. Some of the current limitations and future trends are then highlighted. The combination of these four–part monitoring methods can make the quality of PBF parts highly assured. We unanimously believe that this article can be helpful for future research on PBF process monitoring.

Marco Grasso and Bianca Maria Colosimo. Process defects and in situ monitoring methods in metal powder bed fusion: a review. Measurement Science and Technology, 28:044005, Feb 2017. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6501/aa5c4f, doi:10.1088/1361-6501/aa5c4f. This article has 1253 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt directly compares several coaxial SLM melt-pool sensing approaches. A Concept Laser/KU Leuven system combines a high-speed NIR CMOS camera and a photodiode. A partially reflective mirror directs the 1064 nm laser toward the scanner while transmitting melt-pool radiation at 780–950 nm to the sensors; the incoming radiation can be integrated into a single melt-pool intensity value. The 1280 × 1024 CMOS camera also measures melt-pool shape, size, geometry, and temperature distribution, while both sensors can operate at 10 kHz, subject to the camera’s limited field of view. Other coaxial systems use a two-wavelength pyrometer connected by optical fiber, with two InGaAs photodiodes, a 1200–2900 K range, a 1260 nm central transmission wavelength, 100 nm bandwidth, and a 560 µm measurement diameter. CCD cameras measure brightness profiles, with reported sampling up to 20 kHz. The excerpt also discusses coaxial illumination and a pre-focusing unit designed to mitigate axial and lateral chromatic aberration from f-theta optics across different wavelengths. It does not provide calibration procedures using blackbodies or tungsten lamps, nor specific aluminium-alloy melt-pool temperatures or emissivity analysis.

## pqac-00000009

From text 'sloane2025investigatingthevalue pages 118-122'.

A Sloane. Investigating the value of in-situ monitoring in the laser powder bed fusion of nickel-based superalloys. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt compares coaxial pyrometry and camera-based melt-pool monitoring, emphasizing the role of dichroic mirrors in separating laser and thermal radiation. A 316L study used a pyrometer behind a mirror reflecting 1070 nm while transmitting 1500–1700 nm; its 100 kHz measurements were spatially registered to the galvo position and strongly correlated with porosity. Normalized signals were interpreted as distinguishing conduction, transition, and keyhole regimes. A dual-pyrometer system for AlSi10Mg operated at 200 kHz and detected melting modes, but produced counterintuitive lower temperatures over shallow overhangs because pyrometry collapses melt-pool size, shape, and temperature-profile information into an intensity-derived estimate. The passage highlights the temperature–emissivity circular dependency and identifies multi-wavelength detection as a way to address it, while warning that morphology can still cause misinterpretation. It also describes coaxial visible and infrared cameras: binary visible-light images of melt-pool size and shape predicted porosity with 78–93% accuracy, while an 850–1000 nm camera correlated overheating with swelling defects. The excerpt does not provide information on photodiodes specifically, 1064 nm mirror-coating effects, f-theta chromatic aberration, blackbody or tungsten-lamp calibration, or detailed aluminium-alloy temperature and emissivity values.

## pqac-00000010

From text 'sun2019computationalfluiddynamics pages 53-56'.

Z Sun. Computational fluid dynamics modelling of powder-based laser additive manufacturing processes. Unknown journal, 2019.

The excerpt compares optical approaches for LPBF melt-pool monitoring, although it does not specifically discuss galvo-scanner optical paths, 1064 nm mirror coatings, f-theta chromatic aberration, tungsten-lamp calibration, or aluminium-alloy emissivity. Photodiodes provide fast response, high sensitivity, and straightforward integration; they have been used to measure melt-pool emissions, area, width, and length at sampling rates up to 10–20 kHz, while multispectral photodiode sensing reached 100 kHz. Their limitations include temperature-dependent characteristics and poor temperature stability. Two-colour pyrometry uses two InGaAs photodiodes for non-contact high-temperature measurement. Coaxial installation synchronizes the monitored area with the melt pool and is considered more suitable for real-time in-situ temperature measurement than stationary off-axis arrangements. However, pyrometry can be affected by dust and smoke and lacks spatial resolution. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6501/aa5c4f, doi:10.1088/1361-6501/aa5c4f. This article has 1253 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt directly addresses several optical issues in coaxial melt-pool monitoring. In the described SLM arrangement, a partially reflective mirror is designed to reflect the 1064 nm processing laser toward the scanner while transmitting melt-pool radiation at other wavelengths, specifically 780–950 nm, to the camera and photodiode. Thus, the mirror coating’s wavelength-dependent reflectance/transmittance is fundamental to separating laser light from emitted process radiation and enabling coaxial imaging. The excerpt also notes that f-theta lenses have different imaging properties at wavelengths other than the processing wavelength. This produces axial and lateral chromatic aberrations, which can cause wavelength-dependent focus shifts and image misregistration or distortion. A pre-focusing unit is introduced to compensate for these effects and ensure that the focal plane remains coincident across the wavelengths of interest. Regarding camera limitations, the cited system uses a 1280 × 1024 pixel NIR CMOS sensor, allowing melt-pool geometry and temperature-distribution measurements. However, achieving the stated 10 kHz sampling rate requires reducing the camera’s field of view to a limited region of interest, indicating a tradeoff between temporal sampling and spatial coverage. The passage does not provide quantitative limits for field distortion, residual focus shift, optical resolution, or coating performance.

The excerpt directly addresses how coaxial optical components can constrain imaging at wavelengths different from the laser wavelength. Machine optics are optimized for the working laser wavelength, so galvanometer mirror coatings may strongly suppress monitoring bands; a cited spectrometer test found that 750–875 nm wavelengths were almost completely blocked by the galvanometer scanning-mirror coating. Lenses, mirrors, and filters can also attenuate the selected meltpool-emission wavelengths, while their wavelength-dependent transmission/reflection must be considered when selecting camera bands. The text further notes that different optical-element incidence angles produce different transmitted/reflected intensities, making calibration dependent on the exact positions and orientations of the optics. Regarding coaxial-camera resolution, spatial resolution should be defined at the build plane in µm/pixel and selected relative to the smallest meltpool feature to be quantified. Coarser sampling can prevent meaningful recovery of meltpool shape, boundaries, and internal intensity or temperature gradients; increasing spatial resolution may reduce field of view and acquisition frequency. However, this excerpt does not explicitly discuss chromatic aberration of f-theta lenses, wavelength-dependent focus shift, or field distortion. ## pqac-00000068

From text 'fleming2020trackingandcontrolling pages 10-13'.

Tristan G. Fleming, Stephen G.L. Nestor, Troy R. Allen, Mark A. Boukhaled, Nathan J. Smith, and James M. Fraser. Tracking and controlling the morphology evolution of 3d powder-bed fusion in situ using inline coherent imaging. Additive manufacturing, 32:100978, Mar 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2019.100978, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2019.100978. This article has 105 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports that inline coherent imaging (ICI) in the LPBF system provides an axial (depth) resolution of 7 µm and a transverse (lateral) resolution of 30 µm, with a measurement line rate of 50 kHz that can be increased to 312 kHz. The system measures sample height over an 825 µm depth range by raster-scanning the imaging beam and detecting backscattered light. Its height-measurement repeatability was evaluated on a static mirror over 100 seconds and yielded a standard deviation of 0.30 µm; this is the stated precision/repeatability figure rather than a separately reported absolute layer-height accuracy. The system can image both solid metal and metal powder and captures layer morphology before and after processing. ICI is integrated coaxially with the processing laser: the imaging beam is directed and collected through the same lens as the processing beam, using the same XY galvanometers. This provides a direct top-down view without perspective correction. The excerpt does not report crack-detection capability, so no conclusion about whether ICI detects cracks can be supported from these pages. It instead emphasizes morphology monitoring, roughness extraction, raised-area identification, and layer-height measurement.

## pqac-00000069

From text 'fleming2023synchrotronvalidationof pages 3-4'.

Tristan G. Fleming, Samuel J. Clark, Xianqiang Fan, Kamel Fezzaa, Chu Lun Alex Leung, Peter D. Lee, and James M. Fraser. Synchrotron validation of inline coherent imaging for tracking laser keyhole depth. Additive Manufacturing, 77:103798, Sep 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2023.103798, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2023.103798. This article has 39 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes ICI as an optical measurement method integrated coaxially with the LPBF processing laser. A MEMS scanner aligns the imaging beam with the high-power laser, while a focusing lens, dichroic mirror, and dielectric mirror couple and direct the beam toward the sample. For moving welds and LPBF tracks, the ICI beam was offset to trail the laser by 10 µm so that it centered on the keyhole root, maximizing the average backscattered intensity. Each ICI A-line provides backscattered intensity versus depth, and a depth value can be extracted using maximum-intensity tracking after applying a 13 dB noise threshold. Alternatively, Gaussian fitting tracks the A-line centroid and corresponding height with sub-micron precision, demonstrating high layer-height measurement capability under the stated stability test. The system supports high-speed acquisition: the cited APS setup operated at 140 kHz, with imaging extended to 14 ms and 1260 frames, covering approximately 7 mm of each 9.5 mm track; imaging duration was limited by camera memory. The excerpt does not provide explicit numerical depth resolution, lateral resolution, or dedicated crack-detection capability, although it notes that aluminum 6061’s cracking behavior is useful for imaging defect formation.

The focused imaging-beam spot size is 25 ± 4 µm (1/e²), providing an indication of lateral spatial resolution, although the excerpt does not explicitly define the effective lateral resolution. The ICI system uses a MEMS scanner mirror in a scanning module and an in-chamber imaging module containing a focusing lens and dichroic mirror. This demonstrates optical integration with the LPBF setup and compatibility with the processing beam path; the laser beam is redirected by the ICI imaging module. The excerpt also describes high-speed operation and reports synchrotron imaging at 140 kHz, but it does not clearly state the ICI measurement rate itself. No information is provided here about crack-detection capability or layer-height measurement accuracy. The passage instead focuses on keyhole-depth tracking, keyhole morphology, signal loss, multiple reflections, speckle, and validation against synchrotron X-ray radiography. Therefore, the excerpt supports depth resolution, approximate lateral resolution, and coaxial/in-chamber integration, but not quantitative claims about crack detection or layer-height accuracy.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/tim.2025.3608360, doi:10.1109/tim.2025.3608360. This article has 5 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt describes a coaxially integrated binocular imaging system for in situ three-dimensional LPBF melt-pool and keyhole monitoring, rather than inline coherent imaging (ICI) specifically. Its reported lateral/spatial resolution is 6.20 μm. The measured 3D reconstruction accuracy is 10.6 μm, based on a gauge-block test with a 500 μm depth difference; the reconstructed depth was 510.5 μm and the lateral deviation was 10 μm. Images were captured at 30 ms intervals, while the cropped 512 × 512 binocular images enabled an average 3D reconstruction time of 0.018 s. The system successfully visualized melt-pool morphology and keyholes, with keyhole depths reported from 100 to 130 μm. However, the excerpt provides no specific evidence about crack detection capability or layer-height measurement accuracy. It also does not report a separate depth-resolution value; the closest depth-related performance metric is the 10.6 μm 3D reconstruction accuracy. The optical arrangement was coaxially integrated with the LPBF equipment, using mirrors, right-angle prisms, and a long-working-distance lens to capture the melt pool.

The stated depth/axial resolution is 6 µm, the transverse/lateral resolution is 35 µm, and the measurement rate is 200 kHz. ICI measures track-surface morphology and can capture surface roughness, sintered powder particles, waviness, and humping. Importantly, the study reports in situ recording of the morphology signature of crack openings at the track surface, while simultaneous synchrotron X-ray radiography was used to relate these surface signatures to subsurface cracking. The excerpt emphasizes robustness to high-power laser light and process emissions, and describes integrated scanning and focusing optics within the DED system. It does not provide a numerical layer-height measurement accuracy, nor does it explicitly state that the ICI optics are coaxial with the processing laser; it only establishes inline integration and optical integration into the process setup. Therefore, the excerpt supports resolution, acquisition-rate, morphology-monitoring, and surface-crack-detection capabilities, but does not establish LPBF-specific performance or a quantified layer-height accuracy.

From text 'fleming2020trackingandcontrolling pages 6-10'.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2019.100978, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2019.100978. This article has 105 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt establishes that inline coherent imaging (ICI), based on low-coherence interferometry, is used for in situ, layer-by-layer morphology measurements in powder-bed fusion. It can image both diffuse and specular surfaces, unlike fringe projection, and the system captures full-layer morphology by raster-scanning an imaging beam across the workpiece. Measurements are made on both the deposited powder layer before processing and the consolidated solid layer afterward. The ICI data are used to identify raised regions that may collide with and damage the recoater blade, as well as depressions that may promote pores in subsequent layers. The study further demonstrates morphology-based manual closed-loop correction using targeted laser ablation for raised areas and powder deposition followed by selective remelting for low regions. The excerpt does not provide numerical ICI depth resolution, lateral resolution, measurement rate, layer-height measurement accuracy, or crack-detection capability. It also does not explicitly describe whether the ICI optics are coaxially integrated with the processing laser. A cited fringe-projection system is reported to have 6.8 µm in-plane resolution and 0.47 µm single-point repeatability, but these values are not ICI specifications and should not be attributed to ICI.

ICI A-lines measure backscattered intensity versus height, and Gaussian fitting extracts surface-height centroids with sub-pixel precision. The reported single-point height repeatability was 1.0 µm over 100 ms at 100 kHz and 1.02 µm over 1 s at 10 kHz, providing an indication of layer-height measurement accuracy and temporal stability. The excerpt mentions a 6.67 µm × 6.67 µm/pixel X-ray imaging system, but this is the synchrotron X-ray camera specification, not ICI lateral resolution; no explicit ICI lateral or axial/depth resolution is given. ICI temporal measurements were acquired at 100 kHz and 10 kHz, while the excerpt does not state a complete volumetric or scan measurement rate. Cracking was resolved using X-ray radiographs with VBM4D denoising and histogram stretching; this demonstrates crack-imaging capability in the overall multimodal experiment but does not establish that ICI directly detects cracks. The ICI beam was deliberately positioned off-axis from the processing beam, with independent scanning and focusing optics, rather than being coaxially integrated with the processing laser.

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table ranking monitoring additions for a lab LPBF machine screening aluminium alloys, ordered by priority (what to add first). Columns: Rank, Monitoring Addition, Approximate Cost (USD), What It Teaches (spreading/melt pool/cracking), Key Specifications, Commercial Examples. Include: 1. Structure-borne acoustic emission sensor (~$1-3k), 2. Upgraded coaxial photodiode to second-channel two-colour pyrometry (~$2-5k), 3. Off-axis high-speed camera with illumination (~$5-15k for entry-level), 4. Data acquisition and synchronisation system (NI DAQ, ~$3-6k), 5. Airborne microphone (~$0.5-1k), 6. SWIR thermal camera (~$8-20k), 7. Fringe projection profilometry (~$5-15k), 8. Off-axis layer camera upgrade (already planned). Note that many items have wide price ranges."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Rank | Monitoring addition | Approximate cost (USD) | What it teaches | Key specifications for this machine | Commercial examples |
|---:|---|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Structure-borne acoustic-emission system | $1,000–3,000 for sensor, preamplifier, coupling/waveguide; $4,000–10,000 with dedicated multichannel acquisition | **Cracking:** best affordable direct candidate for detecting crack initiation during scanning and delayed cracking during cool-down; also records recoater impacts and delamination. Seleznev et al. detected CT-confirmed cracks using 50–600 kHz acquisition, although small cracks were missed and no formal false-alarm rate was reported. (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051) | Use a broadband or resonant contact sensor under the aluminium plate; sample at ≥2 MS/s, 16–18 bit, with approximately 50–600 kHz analog filtering and 40 dB preamplification. Record continuously through at least one hour of post-build cooling. Establish pencil-lead-break transfer functions for every plate, temperature, bolt torque, foil and ceramic-break configuration. | MISTRAS/PAC D9215 high-temperature sensor; PAC R15α/R30α with remote waveguide; Physical Acoustics 2/4/6 preamplifier; Vallen VS150-RIC or VS375-M. Prices are budgetary and often quotation-only. |
| 2 | Second coaxial optical channel, initially as ratio photodiode/pyrometer | $2,000–5,000 | **Melt pool:** adds a spectral ratio, improving discrimination between radiance changes caused by temperature and those caused by area/emissivity; retains ≥100 kHz bandwidth. It does **not** measure crack opening directly and can still be misled by plume, geometry and non-grey aluminium emissivity. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012) | Before buying detectors, measure end-to-end transmission through the basiCube mirrors and f-theta lens: coatings optimized for 1064 nm can nearly block some visible/NIR bands. Choose two narrow, nearby bands that both transmit well, exclude 1070 nm and remain within detector response; digitize synchronously at 250 kS/s–1 MS/s/channel. Calibrate the complete optical train with a radiance source, not detectors alone. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000065) | Thorlabs Si or InGaAs photodiodes plus narrowband filters, beamsplitter and transimpedance amplifiers; Hamamatsu Si/InGaAs modules; commercial two-colour instruments from Kleiber, Sensortherm or Dr. Mergenthaler. A custom dual-photodiode channel generally fits this budget better than a complete pyrometer. |
| 3 | Off-axis high-speed camera with narrowband active illumination | $5,000–15,000 entry-level; $20,000–100,000+ for Photron/Phantom and Cavitar-class systems | **Melt pool and spatter:** uniquely shows pool outline, denudation, plume, ejection angle, particle trajectories and surface crack opening when sufficiently large. At 1.1 m/s, 20–50 kfps gives 55–22 µm laser travel per frame; ≥50 kfps is desirable for pool dynamics. Research systems range from 20 kfps/30 µs exposure to 1 Mfps/200 ns exposure. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000023) | Use a replaceable sacrificial window, purge curtain and steep viewing angle compatible with gas flow. Start around 10–30 µm/pixel over a 3–8 mm field, 20–50 kfps and ≤2–5 µs exposure. Add 640, 808 or 810 nm pulsed illumination and a matched 10–20 nm bandpass filter; block 1070 nm with high optical density. Long-working-distance microscopy is more useful than megapixel resolution. | Kron Technologies Chronos 2.1-HD/4K12; used Photron FASTCAM Mini UX/AX; Phantom Miro; Infinity K2 DistaMax or Navitar 12× long-distance optics; Cavitar CAVILUX HF is excellent but often exceeds the entry-level budget. |
| 4 | Common-clock DAQ and synchronization backbone | $3,000–6,000 | **All modalities:** converts attractive videos and waveforms into spatially registered evidence. Enables correlation of crack AE with the responsible track, photodiode transients with commanded position, and layer defects with recoating events. NIST-style datasets register commanded XY/power, encoder feedback, camera trigger and layerwise/XCT data. (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059) | Derive a hardware master clock; capture laser gate, commanded and measured laser power, RTC/galvo X–Y feedback, photodiodes, AE trigger/envelope, camera exposure, recoater state, plate thermocouples, O₂, pressure, dew point and gas-flow proxies. Use hardware timestamps and periodic synchronization pulses rather than PC arrival times. Expect tens of GB per build even for 100 kHz scalar channels plus position data. (pqac-00000044) | NI PCIe/PXIe-6363 or 6353 with BNC-2110/SCB-68A; NI PXIe for expansion; Spectrum Instrumentation digitizers; PicoScope 5000D for lower-cost trials; FPGA/Red Pitaya only if timing and calibration are independently verified. |
| 5 | Wideband airborne microphone or ultrasonic microphone | $500–1,000 | **Process screening:** inexpensive complementary measurement of plume, spatter, recoater and occasional crack-related sound; useful for classifying regimes but less direct and more noise-sensitive than structure-borne AE. Audible crack signatures around 12–16 kHz have been reported in DED composites, whereas conventional solid-borne crack AE commonly extends into hundreds of kilohertz. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006) | Mount outside the direct plume and gas jet, acoustically isolate pumps, and record a reference microphone near the circulation system. Prefer approximately 10–200 kHz bandwidth and ≥500 kS/s. Do not claim crack detection until events are validated against CT/metallography and distinguished from laser switching and recoater impacts. | Avisoft CM16/CMPA with UltraSoundGate; GRAS or PCB Piezotronics measurement microphones; lower-cost ultrasonic MEMS arrays for experimentation. |
| 6 | Off-axis SWIR thermal camera | $8,000–20,000 used/entry-level; $20,000–60,000+ scientific | **Cooling and heat accumulation:** maps the track tail, remelt heating, overhang/substrate effects and layer-scale thermal drift. SWIR generally offers a practical balance of size, speed and sensitivity to cooler material, but an aluminium temperature map remains radiance-based unless emissivity and optical transmission are controlled. (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037) | Prefer InGaAs, approximately 0.9–1.7 µm, ≥500 fps with cropped ROI and externally triggered exposures. Use ND filters to avoid melt-pool saturation. Sapphire or fused silica can serve in much of SWIR after measuring transmission; do not use ordinary fused silica for MWIR. Calibrate through the installed window/cover slide against a blackbody or calibrated radiance source. | Allied Vision Goldeye; Xenics Bobcat/Wildcat; Sensors Unlimited/Collins SU640; used FLIR A6260sc/A6750sc-class cameras, usually above the stated range. |
| 7 | Fringe-projection profilometry or recoater-mounted laser-line profiler | $5,000–15,000 custom; $15,000–40,000+ turnkey | **Spreading and height:** quantifies actual powder/solid topography, streaks, ridges, short feed, swelling and super-elevated edges—information a single intensity image cannot reliably provide. Demonstrated fringe projection achieved approximately 6.8 µm lateral sampling and 0.47 µm single-point repeatability; practical in-machine vertical accuracy is more commonly around 10 µm. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000030) | For 30–60 µm layers, target ≤10 µm vertical uncertainty and ≤25–50 µm lateral sampling. Acquire before and after recoating and after exposure. Use multiple phase shifts/HDR because bright consolidated aluminium and dark powder can coexist. A profiler on the recoater is mechanically simpler but has a narrow swath and must tolerate vibration. | Custom Basler/FLIR machine-vision camera plus DLP projector; Keyence LJ-V7000/LJ-X8000 line profiler; Micro-Epsilon scanCONTROL; Photoneo structured-light systems. |
| 8 | Optimize the already-planned 12 MP layer camera rather than replace it | $500–3,000 incremental | **Spreading:** the planned 26 µm/pixel is adequate for streaks, short feed, recoater damage, spatter deposits and raised edges, but not reliable particle-by-particle inspection of 30–60 µm powder. Side/raking illumination has produced 60–99% anomaly detection depending on defect and machine; 10–13 µm/pixel systems provide stronger pore/texture correlations. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028) | Add two independently strobed raking-light directions, one diffuse top light, cross-polarization, fixed manual exposure and flat-field/reference images. Capture pre-spread, during-recoater if possible, post-spread and post-laser frames. Preserve raw 12/16-bit images and geometric calibration. A second close-up ROI camera is preferable to replacing the full-plate camera. | Existing 12 MP camera plus CCS/Advanced Illumination LED bars, polarizers and strobed controller; optional Basler ace 2, FLIR Blackfly S or Lucid Triton close-up camera. Costs across all rows are approximate 2026 research-market estimates and exclude integration, chamber modification and calibration labor. |

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table summarizing in-situ methods that have actually detected solidification (hot) cracking in LPBF, DED, or laser welding of crack-prone alloys. Columns: Method/Sensor, Alloy System, Frequency Band or Wavelength, Sensor Placement, Validation Method, Key Findings/Limitations. Include rows for:
1. Structure-borne AE (Seleznev 2022, Al92Mn6Ce2 in LPBF, 50-600 kHz, sensor on baseplate, micro-CT validation, detected cracks during build and cooling but some missed)
2. Operando synchrotron X-ray + AE (Fardan 2026, CM247LC in PBF-LB, synchronized radiography and AE, confirmed solidification cracking at high-angle grain boundaries)
3. Inline coherent imaging ICI (Fleming 2023, CM247LC in DED, 6 µm depth resolution, 200 kHz, detected 7 µm crack openings, validated against synchrotron radiography >0.93 correlation)
4. Airborne AE/optical microphone (Nobari 2026 review, DED composites, 12-16 kHz audible signals, optical microscopy validation)
5. Thermal sensing (indirect - no direct crack detection reported; monitors cooling rates and gradients associated with cracking susceptibility)
6. Layer camera imaging (can sometimes see surface-breaking cracks if resolution sufficient, but not demonstrated for hot cracks specifically)"}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Method / sensor | Alloy system and process | Frequency band or wavelength | Sensor placement | Validation method | Key findings / limitations |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Structure-borne acoustic emission (AE) | Al92Mn6Ce2, LPBF | 50–600 kHz analog band-pass; 2 MHz, 18-bit sampling; crack spectra peaked near 100 kHz and extended to about 500 kHz | Broadband high-temperature D9215 piezoelectric sensor coupled directly beneath each specimen on the aluminium baseplate with high-temperature grease; 40 dB preamplification | Ex-situ micro-CT at 2.85 µm voxel size, spatially and temporally correlated with machine logs | Detected millisecond-scale crack bursts during fabrication and post-build cooling, including delayed events. Four CT crack locations in one build had associated AE activity, but three nearby cracks could merge into one event and at least one triple-crack site was missed; no formal sensitivity or false-alarm rate was reported. Pump and machine noise required waveform-based discrimination. (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051) |
| Synchronized operando synchrotron X-ray radiography and bulk AE | CM247LC, PBF-LB; also CM247LC modified with Hf or nano-Y2O3 | X-ray energy/frame-rate and AE passband were not specified in the available excerpt | Thin PBF specimen in the synchrotron beam; AE coupled through the solid specimen or substrate and synchronized with radiographs | Direct operando radiography, supported by post-process microstructure and solidification modelling | Directly confirmed that extensive cracking in unmodified CM247LC was primarily solidification cracking near the terminal stage of melt-pool solidification. Hf and nano-Y2O3 reduced cracking by different metallurgical/process mechanisms. This is compelling physical validation of AE timing, but synchrotron geometry is not representative of a normal bulk build and no detection/false-alarm rate was reported. (pqac-00000000) |
| Inline coherent imaging (ICI) correlated with synchrotron radiography | CM247LC, laser DED | Broadband low-coherence interferometry; 6 µm axial and 35 µm lateral resolution; 200 kHz measurement rate | Off-axis optical head at about 24° to the processing laser, with independently scanned and focused measurement beam | Simultaneous synchrotron X-ray radiography; ICI/X-ray surface-topology correlation greater than 0.93 | Resolved surface crack openings as small as 7 µm in valleys produced by track humping and related the surface signatures to subsurface crack growth or healing. It demonstrates direct optical detection when a crack opens at the surface, but the reported cracks were humping-induced in DED and are not automatically equivalent to every LPBF solidification crack. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000072, pqac-00000074) |
| Airborne acoustic sensing, including microphones, optical microphones and laser vibrometers | Reported mainly for laser DED; a SiC-particle-reinforced 316L example generated microcracking during rapid cooling | Distinct audible component around 12–16 kHz in the reinforced-316L example; conventional crack-related solid-borne AE is more commonly reported around 100–700 kHz, with peaks near 300–600 kHz | Contactless microphone or optical microphone within/near the process chamber; laser vibrometer aimed at the substrate or deposited component | Optical microscopy, liquid-penetrant inspection or other conventional inspection; cracked samples showed voids/surface defects while crack-free samples were smoother | Crack-associated bursts can be separated from process noise with high-pass filtering and time–frequency analysis. Evidence is largely for DED thermal-stress, layer or HAZ cracking rather than rigorously proven LPBF solidification cracking; gas flow, pumps, plume and laser modulation are major confounders, and robust false-alarm rates are generally absent. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005) |
| Thermography or pyrometry | Multiple LPBF/DED alloys; no aluminium hot-crack study in the available evidence directly imaged crack initiation thermally | Typical Si NIR: approximately 0.4–1.0 µm; InGaAs SWIR: approximately 0.95–1.7 µm; two-colour high-speed imaging examples used about 700 and 950 nm | Coaxial for the melt pool or off-axis for the track tail, heat-affected zone and layer-scale heat accumulation | Usually correlated with metallography, CT, process parameters or thermal models rather than direct crack-opening observation | Measures the causal environment—temperature field, thermal gradient, cooling rate, remelting and heat accumulation—not the crack itself. Two-colour Ti6Al4V imaging measured roughly 1–40 K/µs cooling and 5–20 K/µm gradients, but emissivity, plume attenuation, reflections and geometry can make temperature estimates misleading, particularly for aluminium. Treat it as a crack-susceptibility covariate unless independently validated. (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000055) |
| Visible layer or high-speed surface imaging | Potentially applicable to surface-breaking cracks in crack-prone Al and Ni alloys; no direct demonstration of LPBF hot-crack detection was established in the reviewed evidence | Visible/NIR bands depend on illumination and filters; detectability is governed principally by object-side sampling, contrast and crack opening | Off-axis through a protected chamber viewport; layer camera after exposure, or high-speed microscope viewing immediately behind the melt pool | Requires registration to metallography or CT; layer-anomaly studies instead validated features such as streaks, swelling, spatter and porosity | A sufficiently open surface crack can be visible, as the 7 µm ICI result shows, but ordinary layer images mainly reveal secondary manifestations such as dark lines, raised edges or changed reflectance. At 26 µm/pixel, the planned camera cannot reliably resolve typical micron-scale hot-crack openings; it may reveal larger connected or surface-breaking cracks over several pixels. No defensible detection or false-alarm rate for hot cracking is available. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028) |


*Table: Methods are separated into direct crack detections and indirect susceptibility measurements. The table highlights validation strength and the important absence of robust detection and false-alarm rates in most studies.*

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").

filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Please review, with sources, in-situ process monitoring for a small lab-built laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine used to screen aluminium alloys, and rank what to add first. The machine: 500 W single-mode CW Yb fibre laser at 1070 nm, SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (20 mm aperture, mirrors coated for 1064 nm, no camera port), f = 160 mm fused-silica f-theta lens, a 2 in. fused-silica chamber window with a replaceable cover slide, a sealed 280 x 190 x 120 mm aluminium chamber in argon at +5 to +20 mbar with a 2.5-3 m/s cross-flow, interchangeable heated build plates of 25, 50 and 75 mm diameter at up to 200 C, 30-60 um layers, ~75-96 um spot, scan speed up to ~1.1 m/s. Powders: AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, and crack-prone 6xxx, 7xxx and 2xxx alloys with and without grain refiners (Zr, Sc, TiB2), so detecting solidification (hot) cracking matters. Monitoring already planned: (a) a 12 MP layer camera looking through a lid viewport 33 degrees off vertical, about 26 um per pixel over the plate, imaging after each spread and after lasing with a low raking light; (b) a coaxial silicon photodiode picking off 520-985 nm melt-pool emission with a dichroic between the shutter and the galvo, sampled at >= 100 kHz. We want to record what happens in the chamber as fully as possible (high resolution, high frame rate, high magnification), with extensive synchronised metadata, and learn about powder spreading, the melt pool, and when cracking happens during solidification.

Questions:
1. Solidification cracking: which in-situ methods have actually detected hot cracking during LPBF (or laser welding or DED) of crack-prone alloys (Al 6xxx/7xxx/2xxx, Ni superalloys such as CM247LC or IN738LC, others)? For each: sensor type (structure-borne acoustic emission under the plate, airborne microphones, fibre Bragg gratings, thermography, pyrometry, optical imaging, synchrotron X-ray), frequency band or wavelengths, sensor placement, how detections were validated (CT, metallography, operando X-ray), and detection rates or false-alarm rates. When does the crack form relative to the melt pool passing (time and distance), and is it ever visible optically at the surface? Does acoustic emission still work through a heated plate with a ceramic thermal break and bolted or foil interfaces; what sensor temperature limits and waveguides are used?
2. Coaxial melt-pool sensing through a galvo: photodiodes versus two-colour pyrometers versus coaxial high-speed cameras. Which wavelength bands and bandwidths are used, how much do 1064 nm scanner mirror coatings and f-theta chromatic aberration limit coaxial imaging (resolution, field, focus shift), and how are they calibrated (blackbody, tungsten lamp, melting-point references)? What melt-pool temperatures and cooling rates have been measured for aluminium alloys in LPBF, and how reliable is two-colour pyrometry on aluminium given its low and changing emissivity?
3. Off-axis high-speed imaging of the melt pool and spatter in research LPBF testbeds (for example Imperial College/Hooper, LLNL, NIST AMMT, Sandia, MIT, EMPA, PSI): frame rates, exposure, magnification and working distance, long-distance microscopes, illumination lasers (for example Cavitar Cavilux) and filters, viewing angle, and how cameras are mounted and windows protected from metal condensate. What is the cheapest setup that still resolves melt-pool and spatter dynamics usefully?
4. Powder spreading and layer quality: what image resolution and lighting detect streaks, short feed, particle-scale defects and super-elevated edges; what in-situ height mapping (fringe projection, laser-line profilometry, low-coherence or inline coherent imaging, triangulation with the scanner's pilot laser) has measured actual layer thickness, and to what accuracy? Has anyone imaged the spreading itself (the powder heap ahead of the blade) at high speed inside an LPBF chamber?
5. Thermal imaging in a small chamber: NIR, SWIR and MWIR cameras, window materials (sapphire, CaF2, ZnSe, germanium), emissivity problems for aluminium, frame rates achievable, and what thermography has shown about cooling, heat accumulation and cracking.
6. Data and synchronisation: which signals to record (scan-controller position and laser gate, commanded and actual laser power, photodiode, acoustic, cameras, plate temperatures, O2, dew point, gas flow, recoater), how to put them on one clock with a SCANLAB RTC-class controller, typical data rates and storage per build, data standards or schemas used (for example NIST, ASTM/ISO), and documented cases where monitoring data misled.
7. Priorities: for a lab machine with a monitoring budget of roughly 20,000-40,000 USD, rank the additions by what they teach about spreading, melt pool and cracking per dollar, and name specific commercial instruments and their approximate prices where you can.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this multi-faceted question about in-situ process monitoring for a lab-built LPBF machine.

Abstract:
ABSTRACT Growing demand for multi-material Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) faces process control and quality monitoring challenges, particularly in ensuring precise material composition. This study explores optical and acoustic emission signals during LPBF processes with multiple materials, addressing challenges in process control and ensuring accurate material composition. Experimental data from processing five powder compositions were collected using a custom-built monitoring system in a commercial LPBF machine. The research categorised signals from LPBF processing various compositions, enhancing prediction accuracy by combining optical with acoustic data and training convolutional neural networks using contrastive learning. Latent spaces of trained models using two contrastive loss functions, clustered acoustic and optical emissions based on similarities, aligning with five compositions. Contrastive learning and sensor fusion were found to be essential for monitoring LPBF processes involving multiple materials. This research advances the understanding of multi-material LPBF, highlighting sensor fusion strategies’ potential for improving quality control in additive manufacturing. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT

Abstract:
The integrative potential of LPBF-printed parts for various innovative applications depends upon the robustness and infallibility of the part quality. Eliminating or sufficiently reducing factors contributing to the formation of defects is an integral step to achieving satisfiable part quality. Significant research efforts have been conducted to understand and quantify the triggers and origins of LPBF defects by investigating the material properties and process parameters for LPBF-printed geometries using various sensing technologies and techniques. Frequently, combinations of sensing techniques are applied to deepen the understanding of the investigated phenomena. The main objectives of this review are to cover the roles of selective sensing technologies by (1) providing a summary of LPBF metal print defects and their corresponding causes, (2) informing readers of the vast number and types of technologies and methodologies available to detect defects in LPBF-printed parts, and (3) equipping readers with publications geared towards defect detection using combinations of sensing technologies. Due to the large pool of developed sensing technology in the last few years for LPBF-printed parts that may be designed for targeting a specific defect in metal alloys, the article herein focuses on sensing technology that is common and applicable to most common defects and has been utilized in characterization for an extended period with proven efficiency and applicability to LPBF metal parts defect detection.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Mise en œuvre d'un alliage d'aluminium structural par fusion laser sur lit de poudres : étude des mécanismes de fissuration</jats:title>
                <jats:p xml:lang="fr">Dans cette thèse, une analyse de la sensibilité à la fissuration à chaud en fonction (i) des paramètres de premier ordre (puissance, vitesse) du procédé de fusion laser sur lit de poudres (L-PBF : Laser Powder Bed Fusion) et (ii) de la variation de la teneur en soluté (Si et Mg principalement) est présentée pour l'alliage d'aluminium à durcissement structural 6061 (Al-0.8Si-1.2Mg wt%). Le mécanisme de fissuration à chaud est identifié comme une fissuration par solidification sur la base d'observations expérimentales des microstructures. En accord avec des travaux antérieurs publiés sur d’autres familles d’alliages, les fissures se propagent aux joints de grains de fortes désorientations et sont préférentiellement situées au centre des bains de fusion. En utilisant le critère de Rappaz-Drezet-Gremaud (RDG criterion) combiné à des simulations thermiques utilisant le formalisme de Rosenthal, la localisation des fissures correspond aux régions des bains de fusion ou la sollicitation mécanique intergranulaire est la plus élevée lors de la solidification. Des cartes de sensibilité à la fissuration à chaud sont ensuite développées pour prédire de manière simple les variations de sensibilité à la fissuration à chaud en fonction des paramètres du procédé de premier ordre, à savoir la puissance laser et la vitesse de balayage ainsi que des conditions de préchauffage. Les tendances prédites sont qualitativement en accord avec les observations expérimentales. Les résultats permettent de discuter de l'impact des conditions d’élaboration sur la réduction de la fissuration à chaud et également d’identifier les paramètres métallurgiques clés de ce mécanisme de fissuration.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Online quality control of advanced manufacturing processes often utilize process monitoring as a qualification method to reduce or eliminate time consuming and costly destructive and non-destructive tests. The need for process monitoring based qualification becomes more apparent with the advent of laser based additive manufacturing for complex geometries and lot-size-one production. However, the usability of the process monitoring solution heavily relies on the accuracy of the established alignment and assignment of process signals to specific part and defects herein. This research proposes a data fusion strategy for data pre-processing to structure and align multi-source sensor data for improving correlation accuracy in process monitoring. A laser powder bed fusion system equipped with a photodiode-based co-axial melt pool monitoring is used for the study. First, the monitoring system collects photon emission data from the melt pool using photodiodes with high frequency (>100 kHz) which are aligned spatially and temporally using position data (xy-coordinates) of the galvanometer scanner and the laser ON/OFF signals. Next, a clustering approach is used to assign each photodiode signal with the individual parts on the build platform. Finally, correlation between melt pool monitoring signals and part level porosity is studied using micro-computed X-ray tomography (μCT) from a build job containing parts produced under varying process conditions.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Reliable process monitoring is critical for advancing laser powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), as it provides the process information required for corrective control actions to prevent defects such as lack-of-fusion and keyhole porosity. A promising approach for PBF-LB/M process monitoring is coaxial measurement of light emitted from the meltpool area. More than two hundred research studies on coaxial monitoring of the meltpool have been performed, but there is still no validated and reliable method for measuring a suitable variable that could be directly used as an input for high-resolution control of the PBF-LB/M process, enabling process parameters such as laser power and scan speed to be dynamically adjusted not only at the part level, but locally for individual micrometer-scale segments along the scan track. This work reviews existing research studies on coaxial meltpool monitoring and identifies potential future research and development directions toward a standard and reliable meltpool monitoring method. Meltpool depth is identified as a particularly promising control-relevant variable. With the ability to monitor and control meltpool depth, it is possible to avoid undesirable process conditions due to too high or too low energy input, which would result in defects like keyhole porosity or lack-of-fusion. However, only five studies have attempted to estimate the melt pool depth coaxially during the PBF-LB/M process. Despite these attempts, there is no sufficiently validated method for high-resolution coaxial monitoring of meltpool depth in PBF-LB/M. The potential solution seems to be in combining concepts and recent discoveries from two-color coaxial camera- and photodiode-based meltpool area monitoring approaches. Based on the existing literature and hands-on experiences with establishing and working with coaxial monitoring systems, this work also provides guidelines and lists the most common challenges for implementing coaxial monitoring of the meltpool in the PBF-LB/M process.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is a key technology for high-precision manufacturing of complex-shaped metallic components. A detailed understanding of the spatter and melt pool behavior during the process is essential for optimizing the process parameters and improving the part quality. This study presents an observation system that combines ultrahigh-speed imaging at 1,000,000 frames per second (fps) with quad-directional (four-direction) laser illumination. This setup facilitates real-time, high-fidelity visualization of dynamic phenomena such as melt pool evolution and spatter generation, which are difficult to observe using conventional single-direction illumination, by reducing self-shadowing and clarifying feature contours. Using this system, transient melt pool behavior with and without spatter was contrasted across four laser powers of 50, 100, 150, and 200 W and four scanning speeds of 50, 100, 150, and 200 mm/s; under spatter-generating conditions, surface protrusions grew more rapidly and detached as spatter once their velocity and geometry were sufficient to overcome surface tension, whereas under nonspattering conditions, they were reabsorbed before detachment. Image analysis quantified frame-to-frame brightness fluctuations on the melt pool surface as a relative indicator of dynamic surface instability and revealed its dependence on process parameters, particularly the volumetric energy density. The results support a mechanism in which dynamic surface instability promotes spatter formation. This approach provides a powerful tool for in-situ analysis of LPBF and contributes to the development of advanced process control and quality assurance in metal additive manufacturing, including real-time spatter control and process-window optimization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conceptual Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Quad-directional illumination paired with an ultrahigh-speed camera capturing one million frames per second makes rapid changes on the melt pool surface during laser powder bed fusion clearly observable. A simple measure of surface-brightness fluctuation summarizes the degree of surface instability and links it to the energy input per unit volume. When surface bumps grow quickly and maintain a favorable shape, they detach as spatter; under calmer settings they are reabsorbed. These insights help select more stable process windows and refine scan strategies to reduce spatter in metal additive manufacturing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Abstract:
<jats:p>While the majority of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) metal additive manufacturing uses a continuous wave (CW) laser heat source, some commercial applications of LPBF additive manufacturing instead involve the modulation of the laser power on tens-of-microsecond timescales as an adjustable process variable. This article reports the use of in situ, high speed x-ray and optical imaging to probe melt pool fluid flow, defect formation, and nearby powder motion during LPBF with both modulated and CW laser heat sources. We observe melt pool dynamics unique to modulated laser melting even at very high duty cycles that are related to fluctuations in vapor depression depth, complex pore formation mechanisms, and changes to denudation physics when compared to CW melting. These behaviors are present in Ti–6Al–4V, 316L stainless steel, and AL1100 alloys but vary slightly as a function of material, indicating a substantial dependence on the viscosity and surface tension of the liquid metal. While high duty cycles produce weld tracks of comparable quality to CW melting, lower duty cycles introduce substantial defect concentrations. At intermediate duty cycles, careful control of modulation parameters can repeatably and precisely yield one pore per laser pulse, suggesting a method for intentionally inserting engineered porosity at specific sites during an LPBF build.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Cracking presents a major hurdle for processing non-weldable Ni-base superalloys, such as CM247LC, by powder bed fusion–laser beam (PBF–LB). This study directly observes cracking behavior in standard CM247LC and two admixed alloys (CM247LC + 1 wt.% Hf and CM247LC + 1 wt.% nano-Y
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    ) using
                    <jats:italic>operando</jats:italic>
                    synchrotron X-ray radiography synchronized with acoustic emission (AE). Our real-time data confirm extensive cracking in the standard alloy is identified to be primarily solidification cracking. Both Y
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    and Hf additions mitigate solidification cracking, though through distinct mechanisms. Nano-Y
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    addition alters the processing regime from keyhole to conduction mode. Scheil solidification simulations predict a narrower solidification range and lower solidification cracking index (SCI). This indicates that a combination of processing regime shift along with modification in solidification as the primary drivers for crack suppression upon addition of nano-Y
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    , despite increased lack of fusion and complex oxide formation. Hf-addition mitigated cracking via enhanced segregation at interdendritic regions, promoting beneficial carbides and improved liquid backfilling. Scheil simulations for alloy with Hf-addition predicted low SCI compared to standard CM247LC due to increased liquid availability in final solidification stages. These insights highlight that nearly crack-free PBF–LB of non-weldable superalloys can be achieved through both the powder modifications.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The production of reliable turbo machinery, particularly gas turbine blades, is a major global challenge. This capability serves as a key indicator of a nation’s industrial base, technological prowess, and comprehensive strength. Critical components in aircraft engines and gas turbines operate under extreme conditions, including high temperatures, high pressures, and substantial mechanical stresses. Consequently, there is a growing urgency to develop cost-effective and time-efficient repair strategies to enhance engine performance and efficiency. However, many mission-critical parts, especially high-pressure (HP) blades, are prone to severe damage. Moreover, taking equipment offline for blade maintenance and repair is a time-consuming process. It is also highly costly to restore these essential components to full functionality. Since 1996, researchers have focused on applying laser metal deposition (LMD) additive manufacturing technology for high-performance repair and remanufacturing of aerospace engines and industrial gas turbine (IGT) blades. Empirical studies have demonstrated that depositing a high-quality, erosion-resistant protective coating on the leading edge of HP blades effectively extends the service life of turbine blades in both aircraft engines and industrial gas turbines. This study systematically outlines the technical workflow of the proposed methodology and provides a concise perspective on emerging development trends.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Metal additive manufacturing (AM) facilitates the production of geometrically complex components, yet its broader industrial use remains limited by the risk of defect formation and uncertainties in their detection, originating from the highly dynamic and high-temperature process environment. To make additive manufacturing more reliable and establish high-quality parts, it is important to understand how these defects form and how their characteristics appear during the process. This review explains the main causes of common defects, such as cracking, porosity, lack of fusion, and inclusions in metal AM processes, including Powder Bed Fusion and Directed Energy Deposition. It also connects main defect formation mechanisms to the optical, thermal, acoustic, and spectroscopic signals that can be measured during the process. Moreover, it is described how commonly used in situ monitoring systems work and how their signals correspond to melt pool dynamics, vapor plume, particle movement, and the solidification process for each kind of defect. An overview is provided of how data from these systems are analyzed, including the extraction of features from images, the evaluation of temperature fields, and the use of time and frequency domain techniques for various signals. By linking the physics of defect formation to measurable process signals, the interpretation of sensor data is enabled, and potential strategies for monitoring specific problems are outlined. Finally, recent developments are examined, including the integration of multiple sensors, advanced feature-representation approaches, and real-time data interpretation coupled with adaptive control. Together, these directions represent promising advances towards more intelligent and reliable monitoring systems for the future of metal AM.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Welding inspection is a critical process that can be severely time-consuming, resulting in productivity delays, especially when destructive or invasive processes are required. This paper defines the novel approach to investigate the physical correlation between common imperfections found in arc welding and the propensity to determine these through the identification of signatures using acoustic emission sensors. Through a set of experiments engineered to induce prominent imperfections (cracks and other anomalies) using a popular welding process and the use of AE technology (both airborne and contact), it provides confirmation that the verification of physical anomalies can indeed be identified through variations in obtained noise frequency signatures. This in situ information provides signals during and after solidification to inform operators of the deposit/HAZ integrity to support the advanced warning of unwanted anomalies and of whether the weld/fabrication process should be halted to undertake rework before completing the fabrication. Experimentation was carried out based on an acceptable set of parameters where extracted data from the sensors were recorded, analysed, and compared with the resultant microstructure. This may allow signal phenomena to be captured and catalogued for future use in referencing against known anomalies.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Powder Bed Fusion – Laser Beam (PBF–LB) of Ni-base superalloys is highly attractive for components in high temperatures applications, particularly within the aerospace and industrial gas turbine sectors. This interest is due to the high degree of design freedom which allows complex internal cooling channels that significantly improve the component lifetime or enable higher operating temperatures, thereby boosting gas turbine efficiency. However, superalloys containing high volume fraction of γ′, like CM247LC with 60 to 70 vol.%, exhibit poor PBF–LB processibility, suffering from both micro- and macro-cracking, and have poor and anisotropic creep performance. The aim of the thesis is to understand the impact of the intricate relationships between PBF–LB process parameters, cracking, residual stresses, heat treatment, microstructure and creep performance. Using operando synchrotron X-ray radiography, the observed micro-cracking is confirmed to occur during solidification. The micro-cracks are observed at the high angle grain boundaries exhibiting a distinct solidification structure consistent with the solidification cracking mechanism. Solidification cracking is mitigated either through alloy/powder modification or through process parameter optimization with any remnant solidification cracks eliminated through hot isostatic pressing (HIP). However, the presence of macro-cracks, particularly around stress concentrators, is observed after HIP. This macro-cracking is identified as strain age cracking (SAC) due to the γ′ precipitation. SAC is minimized by a tailored HIP using higher pressure before reaching solution treatment temperature. Minimizing residual stress by varying PBF–LB process parameters, including scan strategies, is effective in minimizing SAC. The solution heat treatment developed for cast CM247LC when applied to CM247LC produced via PBF–LB indicated limited grain growth and poor creep performance. A re-designed HIP combined with a solution heat treatment at higher temperature of 1280 °C demonstrates 23% increase in creep rupture life compared to the standard 1250 °C, yielding slightly coarser grains, improved grain boundary decoration, and finer uniform cuboidal γ′ precipitates. Despite this optimization, the creep performance remained inferior to that of the cast alloy. Subsequent tailoring of the PBF–LB process to produce a highly columnar and anisotropic microstructure significantly increased the creep life along the build direction. In summary, this investigation into the PBF–LB of CM247LC demonstrates that the effective mitigation of cracking and improvement of creep performance requires tailored PBF–LB processing and post-processing heat treatment strategies.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) has revolutionized production across industries, yet persistent challenges in defect detection and process reliability necessitate advanced in situ monitoring solutions. While non-destructive evaluation (NDE) techniques such as X-ray computed tomography, thermography, and ultrasonic testing have been widely adopted, the critical role of 3D surface topographic monitoring remains underutilized for real-time anomaly detection. This work comprehensively reviews the 3D surface monitoring of AM processes, such as Laser powder bed fusion, directed energy deposition, material extrusion, and material jetting, highlighting the current state and challenges. Furthermore, the article discusses the state-of-the-art advancements in closed-loop feedback control systems, sensor fusion, and machine learning algorithms to integrate 3D surface data with various process signatures to dynamically adjust laser parameters and scan strategies. Guidance has been provided on the best 3D monitoring technique for each of the AM processes. Motivated by manufacturing labor shortages, the high skill required to operate and troubleshoot some of these additive manufacturing techniques, and zero-defect manufacturing goals, this paper also explores the metamorphosis towards autonomous AM systems and adaptive process optimization and explores the role and importance of real-time 3D monitoring in that transition.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is highly susceptible to process instabilities, and defects generated during fabrication are often irreversible. Although Fringe Projection Profilometry (FPP) has emerged as a cost-effective, non-contact technique for surface metrology in LPBF, existing implementations are largely limited to post-layer inspection and cannot capture the transient surface evolution during active laser processing. In this study, a single-view FPP system was designed, assembled, and integrated into a commercial LPBF machine to enable continuous, time-resolved, in situ 4D (x, y, z, time) monitoring throughout the printing process. The proposed system continuously measures both the freshly spread powder bed and the evolving build surface during contour and infill scanning. Experimental results demonstrate the capability to reconstruct the dynamic evolution of the build surface throughout an entire manufacturing cycle, including powder spreading, contour scanning, infill formation, and layer completion. Furthermore, by registering the reconstructed surfaces of successive layers within a common coordinate system, the layer-by-layer material accumulation process can be digitally visualized and quantified. The proposed approach establishes a time-resolved, in situ 4D surface metrology framework for LPBF and provides a new experimental capability for investigating short-term post-scan surface evolution during additive manufacturing.</jats:p>
