Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) holds promise to efficiently produce metal parts. However, LPBF incurs stochastic melt pool (MP) spattering, which would roughen workpiece in-process surface, thus weakening inter-layer bonding and causing issues like porosity, powder contamination, and recoater intervention. Understanding the consequential effect of MP spattering on layer surface remains difficult due to the lack of process monitoring capability for concurrently tracking MP spatters and characterizing layer surfaces. In this work, using our lab-designed LPBF-specific fringe projection profilometry and an off-axis camera, we quantify the correlation between MP spattering and in-process layer surface roughness for the first time to reveal the influence of MP spatters on process anomaly and part defects. A method of extracting and registering MP spattering metrics is developed by machine learning of the in-situ imaging data. Each image is analyzed to obtain the MP center location and the spatter count and ejection angle. These MP spatter signatures are registered for each monitored MP across each layer. Regression modeling is used to correlate registered MP spatter signature and its processing parameters with layer surface topography measured by the in-situ FPP. We find that the attained MP spatter feature profile can help predict the layer surface roughness more accurately (>50% less error), in contrast to the conventional approaches that would only use nominal process setting. This is because the spatter information can reflect key process changes including the deviations in actual laser scan parameters and their effects. The results corroborate the importance of spatter monitoring and the distinct influence of spattering on layer surface roughness. ABSTRACT Additive manufacturing offers a range of novel applications. Abstract:
Over the past decade, significant research has focused on detecting abnormalities in metal laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) additive manufacturing. Effective online monitoring systems are crucial for enhancing process stability, repeatability, and the quality of final components. Therefore, the development of in situ detection mechanisms has become essential for metal L-PBF systems, making efficient closed-loop control strategies to adjust process parameters in real time vital. This paper presents an overview of current in situ monitoring systems used in metal L-PBF, complemented by ex situ characterizations. It discusses in situ techniques employed in L-PBF and evaluates the applicability of commercial systems. The review covers optical, thermal, acoustic, and X-ray in situ methods, along with destructive and non-destructive ex situ methods like optical, Archimedes, and X-ray characterization techniques. Each technique is analyzed based on the sensor used for defect detection and the type or size of defects. Optical in situ monitoring primarily identifies large defects from powder bed abnormalities, while thermal methods detect defects as small as 100 µm and keyholes. Thermal in situ detection techniques are notable for their applicability to commercial devices and efficacy in detecting subsurface defects. Computed tomography scanning excels in locating porosity in 3D space with high accuracy. This study also explores the advantages of multi-sensor in situ techniques, such as combining optical and thermal sensors, and concludes by addressing current research needs and potential applications of multi-sensor systems.

Abstract:
Real-time closed-loop control of metallurgical processes is still in its infancy, mostly based on simple models and limited sensor data and challenged by extreme temperature and harsh process conditions. Contact-free thermal imaging-based measurement approaches thus appear to be particularly suitable for process monitoring. With the potential to generate vast amounts of accurate data in real time and combined with artificial intelligence methods to enable real-time analysis and integration of expert knowledge, thermal spectral imaging is identified as a promising method offering more robust and accurate identification of key parameters, such as surface temperature, morphology, composition, and flow rate.

Abstract:
The main aim of the study was to analyse the strain rate sensitivity of the compressive deformation response in bulk 3D-printed samples from 316L stainless steel according to the printing orientation. The laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) method of metal additive manufacturing was utilised for the production of the samples with three different printing orientations: 0∘, 45∘, and 90∘. The specimens were experimentally investigated during uni-axial quasi-static and dynamic loading. A split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) apparatus was used for the dynamic experiments. The experiments were observed using a high-resolution (quasi-static loading) or a high-speed visible-light camera and a high-speed thermographic camera (dynamic loading) to allow for the quantitative and qualitative analysis of the deformation processes. Digital image correlation (DIC) software was used for the evaluation of displacement fields. To assess the deformation behaviour of the 3D-printed bulk samples and strain rate related properties, an analysis of the true stress–true strain diagrams from quasi-static and dynamic experiments as well as the thermograms captured during the dynamic loading was performed. The results revealed a strong strain rate effect on the mechanical response of the investigated material. Furthermore, a dependency of the strain-rate sensitivity on the printing orientation was identified.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Significant advances have been made in the field of Additive Manufacturing (AM) across various manufacturing processes. Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is one of the most widely adopted metal AM processes in the industry, which employs energy sources such as lasers to melt powder materials. While the LPBF process offers numerous advantages, such as the ability to produce complex geometries and multiple parts simultaneously, it also presents challenges in the form of defects such as porosity, residual stresses, and cracks that need to be addressed. Conducting experiments to identify and eliminate these defects can be prohibitively expensive, motivating the development of alternative predictive approaches. Numerical modeling and simulation techniques provide a cost-effective alternative to experimental approaches, enabling analyses ranging from thermal histories and microstructural evolution to mechanical property prediction and defect identification in fabricated components. However, such simulations can also be computationally intensive. In recent years, Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms have emerged as viable alternative tools to accelerate process understanding, defect prediction, and parameter optimization. This review provides a comprehensive overview of ML-based approaches applied to LPBF, emphasizing the importance of understanding the underlying physical phenomena that significantly influence data collection, preprocessing, and feature engineering strategies essential for effective model training and validation. It offers a structured framework for researchers seeking to leverage ML methods to enhance predictive accuracy and computational efficiency, particularly through simulation-driven data generation for model development.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Direct laser metal deposition (LMD–DED) is an additive manufacturing (AM) process that is used to build up and repair high-quality metal components. It works by overlapping layers of powder material and melting them with a laser. To get a stable process without defects and to reach, at the same time, high mechanical properties, a robust assessment and control of the process parameters, and above all of their combination, is required. The ideal goal is to assure the online control, to stop or correct the process in case of unexpected anomalies. In this work, a robust online monitoring of the laser metal deposition (LMD–DED) process based on the use of infrared thermography was developed and proposed. After choosing the suitable process parameters, a customized design of experiments (DOE) was set, and the statistical analysis of different thermal features was carried out to develop the most robust models that correlate them with the input process parameters (laser power, scanning speed, and powder flow rate). The proposed procedure was based on the extraction of different thermal features from suited regions of interest (ROI), performing statistical analyses by means of analysis of variance (ANOVA) and building regression models to correlate the process parameters with the thermal behavior. The obtained results demonstrated the possibility to control the process by means of the chosen thermal features, independent of the position of the ROI. Moreover, the possibility to use the models to detect typical AM defects, and anomalies, online directly during the process, has been proved and verified by destructive macrographs carried out on the manufactured coupons.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is an additive manufacturing (AM) technique with growing industrial applications. Variations in laser power, scan speed, and thermal conditions can lead to defects such as porosity, cracks, and deformations. Effective Real-time monitoring and control in LPBF are crucial for ensuring process stability, defect mitigation, and part quality consistency as well as improving production efficiency. Existing LPBF process monitoring and control research often focuses on the performance of the algorithms, such as prediction accuracy and decision-making optimization without addressing real-time implementability and discussing the trade-offs between algorithm complexity and computation feasibility. Evaluation of computational resources is essential for advanced monitoring and control algorithm implementation. For real-time data processing and control, Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) is an ideal computing platform for sub millisecond applications. In LPBF AM, melt pool image (MPI)-based process monitoring with machine learning has been widely studied for part quality prediction and control. This paper conducts computing performance evaluation for FPGA implementation of real-time MPI-based LPBF process monitoring. More specifically, latency and resource utilization are analyzed for various advanced analytical algorithms. Two case studies illustrate this evaluation: (1) High-Level Synthesis (HLS)-based analysis of MP feature extraction and (2) High-Level Synthesis for Machine Learning (HLS4ML)-based evaluation of neural network inference for anomaly detection. These cases demonstrate the applicability of FPGA-based solutions to in-process advanced data analytics during LPBF, providing insights for researchers and engineers to develop scalable and efficient real-time control systems for LPBF.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion exhibits many advantages for manufacturing complex geometries from hard to machine alloys such as IN625. However, a major drawback is the formation of high tensile residual stresses, and the complex relationship between the process parameters and the residual stresses has not been fully investigated. The current study presents multi-scale models to examine the variation of process parameters on melt pool dimensions, cyclic temperature evolutions, cooling rate, and cyclic stress generation and how they affect the stress end state. In addition, the effect of the same energy density, which is often overlooked, on the generated residual stresses is investigated. Multi-level validation is performed based on melt pool dimensions, temperature measurements with a two-color pyrometer, and finally, in-depth residual stress measurement. The results show that scan speed has the strongest effect on residual stresses, followed by laser power and hatch spacing. The results are explained in light of the non-linear temperature evolution, temperature gradient, and cooling rate during laser exposure, cooling time, and the rate during recoating time.

Abstract:
This study aims to measure the cooling rates or, more precisely, the cooling durations of single laser tracks by pyrometry within the laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) process. Two-color, as well as one-color pyrometers are tested within this work. Regarding the second, the emissivity of the investigated 30CrMoNb5-2 alloy is determined in-situ within the L-PBF system in order to measure temperature instead of arbitrary units. This is done by heating up printed samples and verifying the measured pyrometer signal by comparing it to values obtained by thermocouples attached to the samples. In addition, the precision of two-color pyrometry is verified for the given setup. Following the verification experiments, single laser track experiments are conducted. The obtained signals prove to be partially distorted mainly due to by-products such as smoke and weld beads arising from the melt pool. To encounter this problem, a new fitting method is presented and experimentally validated. Melt pools resulting from different cooling durations are analyzed by EBSD. These measurements show areas of extreme deformation or potential amorphization correlating with the cooling durations. The obtained cooling duration can be used for the validation of simulations as well as for the correlation of corresponding microstructure and process parameters.

Unveiling crack mitigation pathways in powder bed fusion–laser beam of cm247lc: an operando x-ray radiography study of hf and nano-y2o3 additions. Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 11:9831-9849, Aug 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-026-01876-5, doi:10.1007/s40964-026-01876-5. This article has 1 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies two in-situ methods used to detect hot cracking during PBF-LB of crack-prone CM247LC: operando synchrotron X-ray radiography and bulk acoustic emission (AE). Synchrotron radiography provides direct, real-time visualization of crack formation and was synchronized with AE in this study. AE sensors detect transient elastic waves propagating through the solid material or build substrate following rapid stress redistribution; relevant events include crack initiation, crack propagation, thermal contraction, phase transformation, and dislocation motion. The excerpt states that AE interpretation can use amplitude, frequency content, and event timing, but it does not provide numerical frequency bands or detailed sensor geometry beyond placement on/through the solid material or build substrate. The radiography studies distinguish cracking during processing and have observed simultaneous solidification and liquation cracks. Solidification cracking occurs near the end of melt-pool solidification, when tensile stresses separate solute-rich interdendritic liquid. The excerpt does not discuss thermography or optical sensing, nor does it report specific validation procedures such as metallographic sectioning or tomography; it emphasizes operando observation as overcoming limitations of post-mortem microscopy.

From text 'nobari2026mechanismssensorsand pages 9-11'.

Sanae Tajalli Nobari, Fabian Hanning, Yongcui Mi, and Joerg Volpp. Mechanisms, sensors, and signals for defect formation and in situ monitoring in metal additive manufacturing. Eng, 7:129, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/eng7030129, doi:10.3390/eng7030129. This article has 7 citations.

The excerpt describes in-situ acoustic emission (AE) and thermal sensing for detecting cracking in metal additive manufacturing, with a specific example from DED-LB/M of SiC-particle-reinforced 316L composites. AE sensors detect elastic waves released by sudden stress relaxation during crack initiation, delamination, or related events; piezoelectric sensors receive waves propagating through the substrate or deposited layers. Hot-cracking emissions are summarized as spanning approximately 100–700 kHz, with peak frequencies around 300–600 kHz, while rapid initiation is associated with bursts at 300–600 kHz and above. Lower frequencies are linked to slower crack growth or process instabilities. In the cited DED example, microcracking during rapid cooling generated a distinctive 12–16 kHz audible signal; high-pass filtering and HPSS separated it from process noise. Validation used optical microscopy, which found voids and surface defects in cracked samples and smooth surfaces in crack-free samples, together with spectrogram comparison. Thermal sensing is presented as recording temperature changes before or during crack formation, but no specific thermography configuration is given. The excerpt does not provide synchrotron X-ray results, detailed optical-sensor placement, exact AE sensor locations, or a definitive timing relationship between hot-crack formation and the melt pool; it only relates cracking to rapid cooling and stress release during or after processing.

It states that piezoelectric or optical microphones can be placed either on the build or in the chamber to capture transient phenomena associated with crack initiation. For crack detection, time-domain features—such as amplitude, RMS, rise time, counts, and acoustic energy—are suitable for real-time monitoring, while time–frequency methods including STFT and CWT capture rapid acoustic transients and crack propagation. The table identifies crack initiation and propagation as typical acoustic-emission monitoring targets, but does not provide specific frequency bands, sensor distances, orientations, or calibration details. Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The metal additive manufacturing industry has experienced significant advancement and growth over the past decades. Powder bed fusion stands out as a promising technology for industries such as aerospace and biomedical due to its ability to produce complex geometries with short lead times. A critical drawback of the technology is the potential for defects to arise, restricting full adoption by these highly regulated industries. Achieving process control remains challenging due to many interacting process variables, coupled with stochastic deviations which can result in defects. While these defects may be detected using ex-situ techniques, this is usually a very costly step. Hence, a critical challenge is the need for in-situ detection of defects to improve quality assurance. Despite the variety of in-situ sensors and defect detection algorithms that are emerging in commercial machines, detection accuracy and efficacy remain problematic. These sensors generate large, complex datasets that traditional pattern detection methods struggle to interpret. This presents an excellent opportunity for machine learning, which can uncover complex patterns in large volumes of multi-modal data. This paper offers a critical review of the current state-of-the-art with respect to in-situ monitoring of the powder bed fusion process. It includes a general overview of the various defect types, as well as analysis of different sensing techniques. Special emphasis is placed on the types of machine learning models employed and the methods used to generate their training data. Key breakthroughs are highlighted, and actionable recommendations are provided for future research and areas of improvement.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Metal powder bed fusion (PBF) is an advanced metal additive manufacturing (AM) technology. Compared with traditional manufacturing techniques, PBF has a higher degree of design freedom. Currently, although PBF has received extensive attention in fields with high–quality standards such as aerospace and automotive, there are some disadvantages, namely poor process quality and insufficient stability, which make it difficult to apply the technology to the manufacture of critical components. In order to surmount these limitations, it is necessary to monitor the process. Online monitoring technology can detect defects in time and provide certain feedback control, so it can greatly enhance the stability of the process, thereby ensuring its quality of the process. This paper presents the current status of online monitoring technology of the metal PBF process from the aspects of powder recoating monitoring, powder bed inspection, building process monitoring, and melt layer detection. Some of the current limitations and future trends are then highlighted. The combination of these four–part monitoring methods can make the quality of PBF parts highly assured. We unanimously believe that this article can be helpful for future research on PBF process monitoring.

The excerpt provides general guidance relevant to thermal imaging in LPBF, but it does not identify particular LPBF camera models, viewing-window materials (sapphire, CaF2, ZnSe, or germanium), frame rates, or specific aluminum emissivity values. It emphasizes that thermal cameras are wavelength- and sensor-dependent rather than universally accurate. Silicon detectors cover approximately 400–1000 nm and are commonly restricted to near-infrared wavelengths above 800 nm because metals near their melting temperatures emit relatively little visible radiation. Silicon sensors are effectively limited to temperatures above about 700 K, while InGaAs sensors covering 950–1700 nm can detect cooler temperatures, potentially making them useful for observing cooling behavior; however, the melt pool may saturate such sensors. Neutral-density filters can adjust the measurable temperature range. Temperature calibration may use the Sakuma-Hattori equation, blackbody furnaces, and in-situ thermocouples, but assumptions of constant emissivity and blackbody behavior introduce substantial errors. The excerpt therefore supports interpreting thermography primarily as a tool for relative thermal signatures, cooling behavior, and process monitoring, while warning that quantitative cooling-rate or defect/crack conclusions require careful wavelength selection, calibration, and emissivity treatment. It does not explicitly discuss heat accumulation or cracking detection.

The excerpt provides general background relevant to LPBF monitoring and data acquisition, but it does not document a complete synchronised acquisition architecture. It emphasizes that melt pools are extremely small—typically tens to hundreds of microns—and change rapidly, making them difficult to monitor over an entire build. Existing printers may monitor some variables, such as oxygen, while many other process variables remain unmonitored because of the required technology. Integrating sensors into machines is difficult because LPBF systems require an inert atmosphere, and adding ports for cables or sensors can threaten chamber integrity; machine modification may also be restricted by intellectual-property concerns. The resulting sensors can generate very large data volumes, making data management a major challenge. The excerpt identifies thermal-emission sensing, thermocouples, and high-speed optical imaging as monitoring approaches. Thermal radiation can be related to temperature through the Stefan–Boltzmann law, but accurate temperature estimation requires material emissivity; camera measurements may therefore provide radiance temperature rather than exact temperature. Thermocouples are useful for local or substrate-temperature measurements but can interfere with powder spreading in powder-bed systems. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addlet.2022.100099, doi:10.1016/j.addlet.2022.100099. This article has 58 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes acoustic-emission monitoring for crack detection during laser powder bed fusion of Al92Mn6Ce2 samples. The broadband high-temperature D9215 AE sensor was coupled directly to the aluminum baseplate below each specimen using Molykote 41 high-temperature grease; no separate waveguide is described, so the excerpt indicates coupling through the heated build plate/baseplate rather than reporting a waveguide arrangement. Signals were amplified by 40 dB, filtered with a 50–600 kHz band-pass filter, and sampled at 2 MHz using an 18-bit PCI-2 board. Events above an individually set 90–100 dB threshold were recorded. Monitoring continued throughout fabrication and for two hours afterward to capture cracking during cooling. Validation was performed using Zeiss Xradia Versa 510 micro-CT, reconstructed and segmented in software; the scans had a 2.85 μm voxel size and revealed cracks with openings at least that size. The excerpt does not provide a quantitative detection rate, false-alarm rate, or a numerical operating-temperature limit for the sensor. It only identifies the sensor as “high temperature” and reports use of high-temperature grease. It also does not mention metallographic validation. CT observations qualitatively corresponded to AE expectations, including anticipated high activity in severely cracked BJ3 regions.

The excerpt reports temperature and cooling behavior measured in laser powder bed fusion of Ti6Al4V. After the final pulse in an overhang and first hatch-line scan, the peak cooling rate was approximately 40 K/µs; solidification took about 600 µs for the overhang and 200 µs for the first hatch line. At a scan-line turn, prolonged laser proximity produced an average cooling rate of 1.5 K/µs and kept the material liquid for over 1000 µs. Calibration used a stabilised tungsten-halogen source (Thorlabs SLS201L) illuminating an integrating sphere inside the build chamber. A calibrated Thorlabs CCS200 spectrometer measured the sphere radiance, which was compared with each high-speed camera’s image intensity to determine the wavelength-dependent constants A1 and A2 in the two-colour-ratio equation. An aperture stop was used to reduce intensity and test camera linearity; Figure 5 relates intensity ratio I1/I2 to temperature. Validation employed a type-C tungsten-rhenium thermocouple in argon, heated by a 330 ms stationary laser pulse approximately 0.5 mm from the junction. Imaging agreed within 1% while the laser was on and remained within 5% at approximately 1900 K after shutoff, with increasing noise as the signal declined. The test material was Ti6Al4V, built on a Renishaw AM250 using a 1070 nm continuous-wave fibre laser focused to a 65 µm spot and power-modulated for point-by-point pulsing. Parameters were: hatching 170 W, 75 µm point distance, 60 µs exposure, 65 µm hatch spacing; inner border 170/75/60; outer border 85/45/40; and overhang 155/75/60/65. Optical transmission constraints led to bandpass filters centered at approximately 700 nm and 950 nm. Because the imaging wavelengths differed from the laser-design wavelength, galvanometer-dependent image offsets caused the melt pool to move within the image plane. For two-colour temperature calibration, a stabilized tungsten-halogen source (Thorlabs SLS201L) illuminated an integrating sphere inside the build chamber. Its spectral radiance was measured with a calibrated Thorlabs CCS200 spectrometer and compared with each camera’s image intensity to determine the wavelength-dependent combined optical, filter, and detector efficiencies (A1 and A2).

Hooper reports that a two-wavelength high-speed imaging thermography method measured melt-pool surface temperatures approximately from 1000 to 4000 K at 100 kHz with 20 µm spatial resolution. The measured cooling rates ranged from 1 to 40 K/µs, while thermal gradients ranged from 5 to 20 K/µm. These values varied with process parameter, component geometry, and scan-path location. Scan-line starts and ends and hatch-direction turns made the melt pool more volatile and affected thermal gradients and cooling profiles. Overhang scans cooled significantly more slowly because the underlying unconsolidated powder had low thermal conductivity, despite reduced laser power. The method was validated against a type C thermocouple. Relevant measurement uncertainties include attenuation by the plume, wavelength-dependent attenuation, changing surface angle, unequal emissivity, and reflected radiation within the vapor-pressure depression, all of which can bias the inferred temperature ratio.

### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Rank | Monitoring addition | Approximate cost (USD) | What it teaches | Key specifications for this machine | Commercial examples |
|---:|---|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Structure-borne acoustic-emission system | $1,000–3,000 for sensor, preamplifier, coupling/waveguide; $4,000–10,000 with dedicated multichannel acquisition | **Cracking:** best affordable direct candidate for detecting crack initiation during scanning and delayed cracking during cool-down; also records recoater impacts and delamination. Seleznev et al. detected CT-confirmed cracks using 50–600 kHz acquisition, although small cracks were missed and no formal false-alarm rate was reported. (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051) | Use a broadband or resonant contact sensor under the aluminium plate; sample at ≥2 MS/s, 16–18 bit, with approximately 50–600 kHz analog filtering and 40 dB preamplification. Record continuously through at least one hour of post-build cooling. Establish pencil-lead-break transfer functions for every plate, temperature, bolt torque, foil and ceramic-break configuration. | MISTRAS/PAC D9215 high-temperature sensor; PAC R15α/R30α with remote waveguide; Physical Acoustics 2/4/6 preamplifier; Vallen VS150-RIC or VS375-M. Prices are budgetary and often quotation-only. |
| 2 | Second coaxial optical channel, initially as ratio photodiode/pyrometer | $2,000–5,000 | **Melt pool:** adds a spectral ratio, improving discrimination between radiance changes caused by temperature and those caused by area/emissivity; retains ≥100 kHz bandwidth. It does **not** measure crack opening directly and can still be misled by plume, geometry and non-grey aluminium emissivity. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012) | Before buying detectors, measure end-to-end transmission through the basiCube mirrors and f-theta lens: coatings optimized for 1064 nm can nearly block some visible/NIR bands. Choose two narrow, nearby bands that both transmit well, exclude 1070 nm and remain within detector response; digitize synchronously at 250 kS/s–1 MS/s/channel. Calibrate the complete optical train with a radiance source, not detectors alone. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000065) | Thorlabs Si or InGaAs photodiodes plus narrowband filters, beamsplitter and transimpedance amplifiers; Hamamatsu Si/InGaAs modules; commercial two-colour instruments from Kleiber, Sensortherm or Dr. Mergenthaler. A custom dual-photodiode channel generally fits this budget better than a complete pyrometer. |
| 3 | Off-axis high-speed camera with narrowband active illumination | $5,000–15,000 entry-level; $20,000–100,000+ for Photron/Phantom and Cavitar-class systems | **Melt pool and spatter:** uniquely shows pool outline, denudation, plume, ejection angle, particle trajectories and surface crack opening when sufficiently large. At 1.1 m/s, 20–50 kfps gives 55–22 µm laser travel per frame; ≥50 kfps is desirable for pool dynamics. Research systems range from 20 kfps/30 µs exposure to 1 Mfps/200 ns exposure. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000023) | Use a replaceable sacrificial window, purge curtain and steep viewing angle compatible with gas flow. Start around 10–30 µm/pixel over a 3–8 mm field, 20–50 kfps and ≤2–5 µs exposure. Add 640, 808 or 810 nm pulsed illumination and a matched 10–20 nm bandpass filter; block 1070 nm with high optical density. Long-working-distance microscopy is more useful than megapixel resolution. | Kron Technologies Chronos 2.1-HD/4K12; used Photron FASTCAM Mini UX/AX; Phantom Miro; Infinity K2 DistaMax or Navitar 12× long-distance optics; Cavitar CAVILUX HF is excellent but often exceeds the entry-level budget. |
| 4 | Common-clock DAQ and synchronization backbone | $3,000–6,000 | **All modalities:** converts attractive videos and waveforms into spatially registered evidence. Enables correlation of crack AE with the responsible track, photodiode transients with commanded position, and layer defects with recoating events. NIST-style datasets register commanded XY/power, encoder feedback, camera trigger and layerwise/XCT data. (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059) | Derive a hardware master clock; capture laser gate, commanded and measured laser power, RTC/galvo X–Y feedback, photodiodes, AE trigger/envelope, camera exposure, recoater state, plate thermocouples, O₂, pressure, dew point and gas-flow proxies. Use hardware timestamps and periodic synchronization pulses rather than PC arrival times. Expect tens of GB per build even for 100 kHz scalar channels plus position data. (pqac-00000044) | NI PCIe/PXIe-6363 or 6353 with BNC-2110/SCB-68A; NI PXIe for expansion; Spectrum Instrumentation digitizers; PicoScope 5000D for lower-cost trials; FPGA/Red Pitaya only if timing and calibration are independently verified. |
| 5 | Wideband airborne microphone or ultrasonic microphone | $500–1,000 | **Process screening:** inexpensive complementary measurement of plume, spatter, recoater and occasional crack-related sound; useful for classifying regimes but less direct and more noise-sensitive than structure-borne AE. Audible crack signatures around 12–16 kHz have been reported in DED composites, whereas conventional solid-borne crack AE commonly extends into hundreds of kilohertz. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006) | Mount outside the direct plume and gas jet, acoustically isolate pumps, and record a reference microphone near the circulation system. Prefer approximately 10–200 kHz bandwidth and ≥500 kS/s. Do not claim crack detection until events are validated against CT/metallography and distinguished from laser switching and recoater impacts. | Avisoft CM16/CMPA with UltraSoundGate; GRAS or PCB Piezotronics measurement microphones; lower-cost ultrasonic MEMS arrays for experimentation. |
| 6 | Off-axis SWIR thermal camera | $8,000–20,000 used/entry-level; $20,000–60,000+ scientific | **Cooling and heat accumulation:** maps the track tail, remelt heating, overhang/substrate effects and layer-scale thermal drift. SWIR generally offers a practical balance of size, speed and sensitivity to cooler material, but an aluminium temperature map remains radiance-based unless emissivity and optical transmission are controlled. (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037) | Prefer InGaAs, approximately 0.9–1.7 µm, ≥500 fps with cropped ROI and externally triggered exposures. Use ND filters to avoid melt-pool saturation. Sapphire or fused silica can serve in much of SWIR after measuring transmission; do not use ordinary fused silica for MWIR. Calibrate through the installed window/cover slide against a blackbody or calibrated radiance source. | Allied Vision Goldeye; Xenics Bobcat/Wildcat; Sensors Unlimited/Collins SU640; used FLIR A6260sc/A6750sc-class cameras, usually above the stated range. |
| 7 | Fringe-projection profilometry or recoater-mounted laser-line profiler | $5,000–15,000 custom; $15,000–40,000+ turnkey | **Spreading and height:** quantifies actual powder/solid topography, streaks, ridges, short feed, swelling and super-elevated edges—information a single intensity image cannot reliably provide. Demonstrated fringe projection achieved approximately 6.8 µm lateral sampling and 0.47 µm single-point repeatability; practical in-machine vertical accuracy is more commonly around 10 µm. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000030) | For 30–60 µm layers, target ≤10 µm vertical uncertainty and ≤25–50 µm lateral sampling. Acquire before and after recoating and after exposure. Use multiple phase shifts/HDR because bright consolidated aluminium and dark powder can coexist. A profiler on the recoater is mechanically simpler but has a narrow swath and must tolerate vibration. | Custom Basler/FLIR machine-vision camera plus DLP projector; Keyence LJ-V7000/LJ-X8000 line profiler; Micro-Epsilon scanCONTROL; Photoneo structured-light systems. |
| 8 | Optimize the already-planned 12 MP layer camera rather than replace it | $500–3,000 incremental | **Spreading:** the planned 26 µm/pixel is adequate for streaks, short feed, recoater damage, spatter deposits and raised edges, but not reliable particle-by-particle inspection of 30–60 µm powder. Side/raking illumination has produced 60–99% anomaly detection depending on defect and machine; 10–13 µm/pixel systems provide stronger pore/texture correlations. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028) | Add two independently strobed raking-light directions, one diffuse top light, cross-polarization, fixed manual exposure and flat-field/reference images. Capture pre-spread, during-recoater if possible, post-spread and post-laser frames. Preserve raw 12/16-bit images and geometric calibration. A second close-up ROI camera is preferable to replacing the full-plate camera. | Existing 12 MP camera plus CCS/Advanced Illumination LED bars, polarizers and strobed controller; optional Basler ace 2, FLIR Blackfly S or Lucid Triton close-up camera. Costs across all rows are approximate 2026 research-market estimates and exclude integration, chamber modification and calibration labor. |

Columns: Method/Sensor, Alloy System, Frequency Band or Wavelength, Sensor Placement, Validation Method, Key Findings/Limitations. Include rows for:
1. Structure-borne AE (Seleznev 2022, Al92Mn6Ce2 in LPBF, 50-600 kHz, sensor on baseplate, micro-CT validation, detected cracks during build and cooling but some missed)
2. Operando synchrotron X-ray + AE (Fardan 2026, CM247LC in PBF-LB, synchronized radiography and AE, confirmed solidification cracking at high-angle grain boundaries)
3. Inline coherent imaging ICI (Fleming 2023, CM247LC in DED, 6 µm depth resolution, 200 kHz, detected 7 µm crack openings, validated against synchrotron radiography >0.93 correlation)
4. Airborne AE/optical microphone (Nobari 2026 review, DED composites, 12-16 kHz audible signals, optical microscopy validation)
5. Thermal sensing (indirect - no direct crack detection reported; monitors cooling rates and gradients associated with cracking susceptibility)
6. Layer camera imaging (can sometimes see surface-breaking cracks if resolution sufficient, but not demonstrated for hot cracks specifically)"}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Method / sensor | Alloy system and process | Frequency band or wavelength | Sensor placement | Validation method | Key findings / limitations |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Structure-borne acoustic emission (AE) | Al92Mn6Ce2, LPBF | 50–600 kHz analog band-pass; 2 MHz, 18-bit sampling; crack spectra peaked near 100 kHz and extended to about 500 kHz | Broadband high-temperature D9215 piezoelectric sensor coupled directly beneath each specimen on the aluminium baseplate with high-temperature grease; 40 dB preamplification | Ex-situ micro-CT at 2.85 µm voxel size, spatially and temporally correlated with machine logs | Detected millisecond-scale crack bursts during fabrication and post-build cooling, including delayed events. Four CT crack locations in one build had associated AE activity, but three nearby cracks could merge into one event and at least one triple-crack site was missed; no formal sensitivity or false-alarm rate was reported. Pump and machine noise required waveform-based discrimination. (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051) |
| Synchronized operando synchrotron X-ray radiography and bulk AE | CM247LC, PBF-LB; also CM247LC modified with Hf or nano-Y2O3 | X-ray energy/frame-rate and AE passband were not specified in the available excerpt | Thin PBF specimen in the synchrotron beam; AE coupled through the solid specimen or substrate and synchronized with radiographs | Direct operando radiography, supported by post-process microstructure and solidification modelling | Directly confirmed that extensive cracking in unmodified CM247LC was primarily solidification cracking near the terminal stage of melt-pool solidification. Hf and nano-Y2O3 reduced cracking by different metallurgical/process mechanisms. This is compelling physical validation of AE timing, but synchrotron geometry is not representative of a normal bulk build and no detection/false-alarm rate was reported. (pqac-00000000) |
| Inline coherent imaging (ICI) correlated with synchrotron radiography | CM247LC, laser DED | Broadband low-coherence interferometry; 6 µm axial and 35 µm lateral resolution; 200 kHz measurement rate | Off-axis optical head at about 24° to the processing laser, with independently scanned and focused measurement beam | Simultaneous synchrotron X-ray radiography; ICI/X-ray surface-topology correlation greater than 0.93 | Resolved surface crack openings as small as 7 µm in valleys produced by track humping and related the surface signatures to subsurface crack growth or healing. It demonstrates direct optical detection when a crack opens at the surface, but the reported cracks were humping-induced in DED and are not automatically equivalent to every LPBF solidification crack. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000072, pqac-00000074) |
| Airborne acoustic sensing, including microphones, optical microphones and laser vibrometers | Reported mainly for laser DED; a SiC-particle-reinforced 316L example generated microcracking during rapid cooling | Distinct audible component around 12–16 kHz in the reinforced-316L example; conventional crack-related solid-borne AE is more commonly reported around 100–700 kHz, with peaks near 300–600 kHz | Contactless microphone or optical microphone within/near the process chamber; laser vibrometer aimed at the substrate or deposited component | Optical microscopy, liquid-penetrant inspection or other conventional inspection; cracked samples showed voids/surface defects while crack-free samples were smoother | Crack-associated bursts can be separated from process noise with high-pass filtering and time–frequency analysis. Evidence is largely for DED thermal-stress, layer or HAZ cracking rather than rigorously proven LPBF solidification cracking; gas flow, pumps, plume and laser modulation are major confounders, and robust false-alarm rates are generally absent. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005) |
| Thermography or pyrometry | Multiple LPBF/DED alloys; no aluminium hot-crack study in the available evidence directly imaged crack initiation thermally | Typical Si NIR: approximately 0.4–1.0 µm; InGaAs SWIR: approximately 0.95–1.7 µm; two-colour high-speed imaging examples used about 700 and 950 nm | Coaxial for the melt pool or off-axis for the track tail, heat-affected zone and layer-scale heat accumulation | Usually correlated with metallography, CT, process parameters or thermal models rather than direct crack-opening observation | Measures the causal environment—temperature field, thermal gradient, cooling rate, remelting and heat accumulation—not the crack itself. Two-colour Ti6Al4V imaging measured roughly 1–40 K/µs cooling and 5–20 K/µm gradients, but emissivity, plume attenuation, reflections and geometry can make temperature estimates misleading, particularly for aluminium. Treat it as a crack-susceptibility covariate unless independently validated. (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000055) |
| Visible layer or high-speed surface imaging | Potentially applicable to surface-breaking cracks in crack-prone Al and Ni alloys; no direct demonstration of LPBF hot-crack detection was established in the reviewed evidence | Visible/NIR bands depend on illumination and filters; detectability is governed principally by object-side sampling, contrast and crack opening | Off-axis through a protected chamber viewport; layer camera after exposure, or high-speed microscope viewing immediately behind the melt pool | Requires registration to metallography or CT; layer-anomaly studies instead validated features such as streaks, swelling, spatter and porosity | A sufficiently open surface crack can be visible, as the 7 µm ICI result shows, but ordinary layer images mainly reveal secondary manifestations such as dark lines, raised edges or changed reflectance. At 26 µm/pixel, the planned camera cannot reliably resolve typical micron-scale hot-crack openings; it may reveal larger connected or surface-breaking cracks over several pixels. No defensible detection or false-alarm rate for hot cracking is available. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028) |

{"answer": "# In-Situ Process Monitoring for a Small Lab-Built LPBF Machine Screening Aluminium Alloys

## 1. Solidification Cracking Detection

### Which methods have actually detected hot cracking in-situ?

The following table summarises the in-situ methods for which credible solidification-cracking evidence exists in the published literature:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Structure-borne acoustic emission (AE)** is the most accessible laboratory method. Seleznev et al. coupled a broadband high-temperature D9215 piezoelectric sensor to the aluminium baseplate beneath LPBF-built Al₉₂Mn₆Ce₂ specimens using high-temperature grease, with 40 dB preamplification, a 50–600 kHz band-pass filter, and 2 MHz / 18-bit sampling (pqac-00000047). Crack-related waveforms were triangular bursts of 1–3 ms duration with spectra peaking near 100 kHz and extending to approximately 500 kHz (pqac-00000048). Validation against Zeiss Xradia Versa 510 micro-CT at 2.85 µm voxel size showed all four CT-identified crack locations in one build were associated with AE activity, but a triple-crack site produced only one detected event, possibly because the cracks occurred simultaneously or fell below the 90–100 dB threshold (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049). Crucially, a substantial proportion of crack signals occurred during the first five minutes after build initiation and also during post-build cooling, with crack formation potentially delayed by up to an hour after the responsible layer was built (pqac-00000051). No formal detection rate or false-alarm rate was reported, and the inert-gas circulation pump was a significant noise source requiring waveform-based discrimination (pqac-00000049).

**Regarding AE through a heated plate with thermal breaks:** The Seleznev study coupled the sensor directly to the aluminium baseplate through high-temperature grease, with the sensor described as "high-temperature" but with no stated operating temperature limit (pqac-00000047). For the described machine's ceramic thermal break and bolted/foil interfaces, one should expect significant ultrasonic attenuation and mode conversion at each interface. Practical approaches include: (a) coupling a waveguide rod directly to the build plate below the thermal break, bringing the signal to a sensor at a cooler location; (b) using a high-temperature sensor rated to ≥200–300 °C (the MISTRAS D9215 is rated to approximately 500 °C Curie temperature); and (c) establishing a pencil-lead-break transfer function for every plate/gasket/bolt configuration to verify that crack-frequency signals propagate with detectable amplitude.

**Operando synchrotron X-ray radiography** synchronized with AE on CM247LC confirmed that micro-cracking occurs during solidification, primarily at high-angle grain boundaries near the terminal solidification stage, and that both Hf and nano-Y₂O₃ additions mitigate cracking through distinct mechanisms (pqac-00000000). This approach provides definitive physical validation but requires beamline access and thin-specimen geometry unrepresentative of bulk builds.

**Inline coherent imaging (ICI)** detected surface crack openings as small as 7 µm in humped CM247LC DED tracks, with an off-axis head at 24° and <10 µm lateral registration accuracy. ICI surface-topology measurements correlated >0.93 with synchrotron radiography (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000072). Although demonstrated in DED rather than LPBF, ICI can in principle be integrated coaxially in LPBF systems.

**Airborne acoustic sensing** has captured 12–16 kHz audible signals from microcracking in SiC-reinforced 316L DED composites (pqac-00000001), but this evidence is from DED thermal-stress cracking rather than rigorously proven LPBF solidification cracking.

**Thermal sensing** does not detect the crack itself but monitors the causal thermal environment—gradients, cooling rates, and heat accumulation—and can serve as a cracking-susceptibility covariate (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034).

**Crack timing relative to the melt pool:** Solidification cracking occurs near the terminal stage of solidification when tensile stresses separate solute-rich interdendritic liquid (pqac-00000000). In the AE data, some cracks formed during the build (within seconds of lasing the responsible layer) while others were delayed by minutes to an hour during post-build cooling (pqac-00000051). The melt-pool tail in Ti6Al4V extends approximately 400–1000 µm behind the laser and solidifies in 200–600+ µs (pqac-00000057), suggesting that solidification cracks open within millimetres of the melt pool. Surface visibility depends on crack opening; ICI resolved 7 µm openings (pqac-00000003), but typical LPBF hot cracks in aluminium alloys may remain smaller and subsurface.

---

## 2. Coaxial Melt-Pool Sensing Through a Galvo Scanner

### Photodiodes vs. two-colour pyrometers vs. cameras

The planned single-channel silicon photodiode (520–985 nm, ≥100 kHz) is a proven baseline. Photodiodes offer fast response, high sensitivity and straightforward integration, with demonstrated sampling rates of 10–100+ kHz (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000045). However, a single broad-band channel conflates temperature, melt-pool area, emissivity and plume effects into one scalar signal.

**Two-colour (ratio) pyrometry** adds a second spectral channel and uses the intensity ratio to reduce emissivity dependence. A system by Hooper (2018) used two Photron FASTCAM SA5 cameras with ~700 nm and ~950 nm bandpass filters at up to 200,000 fps and 128×128 pixels on a Renishaw AM250, measuring Ti6Al4V melt-pool temperatures from approximately 1000 to 4000 K with cooling rates of 1–40 K/µs and thermal gradients of 5–20 K/µm (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056). Calibration used a stabilised tungsten-halogen source (Thorlabs SLS201L) illuminating an integrating sphere inside the build chamber, with radiance verified by a calibrated spectrometer; validation against a type-C thermocouple showed agreement within 1% while the laser was on and 5% at ~1900 K after shutoff (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054). A simpler two-InGaAs-photodiode pyrometer has been demonstrated at 1260 nm centre wavelength, 100 nm bandwidth, 1200–2900 K range, and 560 µm spot (pqac-00000008).

**For aluminium alloys**, two-colour pyrometry faces serious challenges. Aluminium has very low emissivity (~0.1–0.2 for liquid) that changes rapidly with oxide state, temperature and phase. A dual-pyrometer study on AlSi10Mg at 200 kHz detected melting modes but produced counterintuitive lower temperatures over shallow overhangs because the signal collapses melt-pool size, shape and temperature-profile information (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012). The low emissivity means weak thermal emission in the NIR, compounding signal-to-noise challenges.

### Effects of 1064 nm galvo mirror coatings and f-theta chromatic aberration

The basiCube 20 mirrors are coated for 1064 nm. Kozjek et al. (2026) note that galvanometer mirror coatings optimised for the working laser wavelength can strongly suppress other bands: a spectrometer test found that wavelengths in the 750–875 nm range were "almost completely blocked" by one scanner's mirror coating (pqac-00000064). Therefore, **before purchasing any coaxial sensor, the end-to-end spectral transmission through the actual basiCube mirrors and f-theta lens must be measured**—ideally with a broadband source and fibre spectrometer at multiple scan positions.

The f-theta lens is designed for 1064 nm; at other wavelengths, chromatic aberration produces wavelength-dependent focal shift and lateral image offset. Hooper noted that imaging at ~700 and ~950 nm through a 1064-nm-optimised scan head required independent camera-position adjustment for the two channels, and that galvanometer-dependent image offsets had to be mapped and corrected as a function of build-plate position and wavelength (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000066). The focal distance also varies with scan position in the build plane (pqac-00000065). A pre-focusing unit can partially compensate (pqac-00000063), but coaxial camera imaging through a basiCube without a camera port will likely be limited to low-resolution intensity collection rather than sharp spatial imaging of the melt pool.

**Practical recommendation for this machine:** Since the basiCube 20 has no camera port and the mirrors may severely attenuate visible/NIR, the most robust coaxial upgrade is a second photodiode channel at a wavelength that transmits adequately, creating a custom two-channel ratio monitor. Measure the actual mirror transmission first, then select two narrow bands that both pass, avoid 1070 nm, and fall within InGaAs or Si detector response (pqac-00000064, pqac-00000065).

---

## 3. Off-Axis High-Speed Imaging of Melt Pool and Spatter

Research LPBF testbeds have demonstrated a wide range of off-axis high-speed imaging configurations:

- **Ultrahigh-speed (1 Mfps):** Sakai et al. used a Shimadzu HPV-X2 at 1,000,000 fps with 200 ns shutter, 400×250 pixels, and a 20× Mitutoyo M-PLAN NIR infinity-corrected objective. Illumination was a Cavitar CAVILUX HF at 640 nm with a 60 ns pulse and four-direction beam splitting; a 645±10 nm bandpass filter was used. The illumination source was 23 cm from the sample (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000023).

- **LLNL testbed:** Calta et al. used an 810 nm pulsed laser (500 W peak, Cavitar) for coaxial illumination and high-speed X-ray + optical imaging (pqac-00000022 context from paper search results).

- **Off-axis thermal/visible cameras at moderate speed:** Thanki used a Mikrotron Eosens 3CL at 20,000 fps, 120×120 pixels, 100 µm/pixel, 30 µs exposure, 25° from vertical, with a 975 nm short-pass filter (pqac-00000019). Mitchell et al. used two cameras at 6500 fps, 65×80 pixels, 21 µm/pixel, with 750 nm and 900 nm filters (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000021). Lough et al. used off-axis IR at 2500 fps with a 1450 nm filter and 130 µm/pixel (pqac-00000017).

- **DED illuminated imaging:** An 808 nm illumination laser with 10 µs pulse and 810±10 nm bandpass filter was used at 100 fps/150 µs exposure, with the camera 320 mm from the nozzle at 30° (pqac-00000022).

**Window protection from condensate:** The 2-inch fused-silica window with a replaceable cover slide is essential. Metal condensate from aluminium alloys is aggressive; the cover slide should be replaced frequently. A gas curtain or laminar-flow screen across the viewing window helps. Steep viewing angles reduce condensate deposition.

**Cheapest useful setup:** An entry-level high-speed camera (Kron Chronos 2.1-HD at ~$5,000–7,000, capable of ~20 kfps at reduced resolution) paired with a used 808 or 850 nm CW diode illumination module (~$300–1,000) and a matched 10 nm bandpass filter (~$200), plus a long-working-distance zoom lens (Navitar 12× or similar, ~$1,500–3,000), can resolve melt-pool shape and gross spatter dynamics at 10–20 µm/pixel over a few-millimetre field. This would cost approximately $7,000–12,000 total. A Cavitar CAVILUX HF system (~$30,000–50,000+) is superior for pulsed illumination and freeze-frame quality but exceeds the stated budget.

---

## 4. Powder Spreading and Layer Quality

### Image resolution and lighting for defect detection

Scime et al. demonstrated that side-lighting and low camera angles produce high contrast, with 60–99% anomaly detection depending on defect type and machine; pre-recoat images target spatter and porosity, post-recoat images target swelling, incomplete spreading and recoater streaking (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028). Lu et al. used a Nikon DSLR with white LED illumination at 10–13 µm/pixel, achieving Pearson correlation up to 0.78 between pixel intensity and XCT-detected pores (pqac-00000024). An inline powder scanner at ~5 µm resolution detected powder unevenness, ultra-high edges and grooves (pqac-00000025).

The planned 12 MP camera at ~26 µm/pixel is adequate for streaks, short feed, raised edges and spatter deposits. It will not resolve individual 30–60 µm particles reliably. Adding two independently strobed raking-light directions and one diffuse top light, plus HDR/flat-field calibration, will maximise contrast.

### In-situ height mapping

**Fringe projection profilometry (FPP)** has been integrated into LPBF chambers. Zhang et al. (2016) achieved approximately 6.8 µm lateral sampling and 0.47 µm single-point height repeatability on a 28×15 mm field, resolving 28 µm peak-to-valley recoater waviness and detecting fused material protruding above the powder level (pqac-00000027). Practical in-machine vertical accuracy is more commonly ~10 µm; IN-718 builds measured part edges to within 100 µm laterally and surfaces to within 10 µm vertically (pqac-00000024). Multi-phase-shift FPP requires several images per measurement, limiting real-time capability but feasible for inter-layer inspection (pqac-00000030).

**Inline coherent imaging (ICI)** provides 7 µm axial resolution, 25–35 µm lateral resolution, and measurement rates from 50 kHz to 312 kHz (pqac-00000068, pqac-00000070). Single-point height repeatability is 0.30 µm over 100 seconds (pqac-00000068). ICI scans coaxially through the processing optics and has been used to detect raised regions, depressions, recoater-blade damage (striations in powder layers) and to perform closed-loop correction of surface roughness with a 54% reduction in maximum roughness (pqac-00000073). However, ICI integration requires coupling into the laser beam path, which is complex with the basiCube 20.

**Low-coherence scanning interferometry (LCSI)** at LLNL produced powder-bed height maps at 100 µm lateral spacing and 25 µm vertical resolution, sampling at 100 kHz (pqac-00000024).

**Recoater-mounted laser-line profilometry** (e.g., Keyence LJ-V7060) provides micron-level surface mapping over a 15 mm swath, detecting gouges, ridges and super-elevated features, though it did not report numerical accuracy (pqac-00000029).

**Imaging the spreading process itself** at high speed inside a chamber has not been convincingly demonstrated in the reviewed literature. Eschner et al. tracked individual powder particles with a two-camera stereoscopic system (pqac-00000026), but this assessed particle motion rather than the powder heap ahead of the blade.

---

## 5. Thermal Imaging in a Small Chamber

### Camera types and spectral ranges

Three spectral ranges are relevant, with distinct trade-offs:

- **NIR (Si detector, ~400–1000 nm):** Silicon sensors are limited to temperatures above ~700 K (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036). They offer high resolution and frame rates (up to 200,000 fps for scientific cameras) and use standard fused-silica or B270 glass windows, making them compatible with the existing chamber window. However, they cannot see the cooling track below red heat.

- **SWIR (InGaAs, ~0.9–1.7 µm):** More sensitive to cooler material, allowing observation of the cooling track tail and heat accumulation patterns. SWIR cameras are more compact and affordable than MWIR and are recommended as the practical choice for integration into small chambers (pqac-00000037). The existing fused-silica window transmits adequately to ~2 µm. Frame rates of 500+ fps with cropped ROI are typical. The melt pool may saturate; ND filters are needed (pqac-00000036).

- **MWIR (3–5 µm):** Best sensitivity to near-ambient and moderate temperatures and can capture full-layer thermal maps. However, fused silica is opaque at MWIR wavelengths—a sapphire, CaF₂ or ZnSe window would be required, adding cost and complexity. MWIR cameras are also more expensive. Altenburg et al. concluded that SWIR and MWIR provide more useful temporal and spatial temperature information than VIS cameras (pqac-00000037).

### Aluminium emissivity challenges

Emissivity of aluminium varies strongly with oxide state, temperature, wavelength, phase (powder vs. liquid vs. solid), and surface condition (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036). Liquid aluminium has very low emissivity (~0.1–0.2), producing weak thermal emission relative to steel or titanium at the same temperature. The result is that any single-wavelength thermal measurement is essentially a radiance measurement, not a temperature measurement, unless emissivity is independently known or controlled. Two-colour pyrometry reduces but does not eliminate this problem, particularly when the emissivity ratio varies with temperature (non-grey behaviour) (pqac-00000055). For aluminium LPBF, thermography should be treated as a tool for relative comparisons (track-to-track, layer-to-layer, region-to-region) and thermal trending, not for absolute temperature measurement.

### What thermography reveals

Thermal imaging has shown heat accumulation in overhangs and thin walls (slower cooling, longer melt-pool tails), geometry-dependent cooling rates, and thermal-gradient variation with scan strategy (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000057). It can identify locations likely susceptible to cracking by virtue of anomalous thermal history, but no reviewed study directly imaged crack formation thermally. In Ti6Al4V, Hooper measured cooling rates of 1–40 K/µs and thermal gradients of 5–20 K/µm, with overhang scans showing greatly reduced cooling and prolonged solidification (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000055).

---

## 6. Data and Synchronisation

### Signals to record

The NIST AMMT architecture provides a reference model. It records: commanded XY position and power (XYPT format, 10 µs between points), DAQ-measured galvanometer X/Y encoder feedback, laser modulation (gate), analog laser power (sampled at 25 kHz), coaxial melt-pool camera images with hardware triggers, layerwise images under multiple LED positions, oxygen sensor, and thermocouple readings (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000061). For the described machine, the full signal list should include: scan-controller XY commands and laser gate from the SCANLAB RTC interface, actual galvo encoder positions, commanded and measured laser power, coaxial photodiode(s), acoustic emission (raw waveform and/or parameterised hits), off-axis cameras (layer and high-speed), plate thermocouples, chamber O₂, dew point, pressure, and gas-flow proxy (anemometer or differential pressure).

### Synchronisation

A 500 µs digital synchronisation pulse triggered sensors in the NASA/NIST testbed, with camera exposure timing combined with the trigger to determine scan position (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000059). Exact temporal synchronisation between galvo-scanner commands and monitoring measurements is essential for high-resolution spatially resolved data; the SCANLAB RTC controller can output a position-synchronised trigger signal. At 100 kHz photodiode sampling and 1.1 m/s scan speed, samples are separated by ~11 µm along the scan path—commensurate with the melt-pool scale. Use hardware timestamps rather than PC arrival times.

### Data rates and storage

Kozjek et al. estimated that a typical PBF-LB/M build using one photodiode plus laser and galvo position data at 100 kHz generates tens of gigabytes (pqac-00000044). Adding raw AE waveforms at 2 MS/s and high-speed camera frames will increase this substantially; a small build might produce 50–200 GB, while extensive instrumentation on larger builds can exceed 1 TB.

### Standards and misleading data

The NIST AMMT datasets are publicly available from data.nist.gov and represent a de facto reference format using registered CSV files with per-layer, per-part structure (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000062). ASTM F3490 (AM data package) and ISO/ASTM 52942 (qualification) address data requirements at a higher level but do not prescribe signal-level schemas. Documented cases of misleading data include: (a) coaxial pyrometry on AlSi10Mg overhangs producing counterintuitive lower temperatures for hotter, narrower, deeper melt pools because the signal conflates geometry and temperature (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012); (b) emissivity-related errors in absolute temperature measurements (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000046); and (c) coaxial-only monitoring missing process signatures outside the melt pool (pqac-00000046).

---

## 7. Priority Ranking

The following table ranks monitoring additions by what they teach about spreading, melt pool and cracking per dollar, given the described machine constraints and a budget of approximately $20,000–40,000.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### Rationale for the ranking

**Acoustic emission ranks first** because it is the only affordable sensor that has been demonstrated to detect crack initiation in-situ during LPBF of a crack-prone aluminium alloy, including delayed cracking during post-build cooling—information that no other sensor provides at any price (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000051). It is also inexpensive and minimally invasive.

**The second coaxial channel ranks second** because it upgrades the already-planned photodiode from an intensity monitor (sensitive to every confound) to a ratio measurement with reduced emissivity dependence, at modest cost (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012). However, the basiCube mirror coatings may limit wavelength choices and require careful spectral characterisation before purchase (pqac-00000064).

**Off-axis high-speed imaging ranks third** because it provides direct visual evidence of melt-pool shape, spatter, plume, denudation and potentially surface cracks—information essential for understanding aluminium LPBF phenomenology and correlating with the other scalar sensors (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019). An entry-level system is achievable within the budget.

**The DAQ/synchronisation backbone ranks fourth** because without it, the other sensors produce interesting but unregistered data that cannot be correlated spatially or temporally with specific tracks, layers and defects (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000058).

A complete first-tier instrumentation package (AE system + second photodiode channel + entry-level high-speed camera + DAQ backbone + airborne microphone + layer camera lighting upgrades) can plausibly fit within $15,000–25,000, leaving headroom for a SWIR camera or fringe projection as a second-tier addition.

**Within a $20,000–40,000 total budget**, items 1–5 and 8 (the incremental layer-camera upgrade) can be achieved, with either item 6 (SWIR camera) or item 7 (fringe projection) depending on whether thermal mapping or height mapping is prioritised. For crack-prone aluminium alloy screening specifically, the SWIR camera is arguably more informative than fringe projection because it reveals cooling-rate and heat-accumulation anomalies that drive cracking susceptibility."}
