# In-Situ Process Monitoring for a Small Lab-Built LPBF Machine Screening Aluminium Alloys

## 1. Solidification Cracking Detection

### Which methods have actually detected hot cracking in-situ?

The following table summarises the in-situ methods for which credible solidification-cracking evidence exists in the published literature:

| Method / sensor | Alloy system and process | Frequency band or wavelength | Sensor placement | Validation method | Key findings / limitations |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Structure-borne acoustic emission (AE) | Al92Mn6Ce2, LPBF | 50–600 kHz analog band-pass; 2 MHz, 18-bit sampling; crack spectra peaked near 100 kHz and extended to about 500 kHz | Broadband high-temperature D9215 piezoelectric sensor coupled directly beneath each specimen on the aluminium baseplate with high-temperature grease; 40 dB preamplification | Ex-situ micro-CT at 2.85 µm voxel size, spatially and temporally correlated with machine logs | Detected millisecond-scale crack bursts during fabrication and post-build cooling, including delayed events. Four CT crack locations in one build had associated AE activity, but three nearby cracks could merge into one event and at least one triple-crack site was missed; no formal sensitivity or false-alarm rate was reported. Pump and machine noise required waveform-based discrimination. (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051) |
| Synchronized operando synchrotron X-ray radiography and bulk AE | CM247LC, PBF-LB; also CM247LC modified with Hf or nano-Y2O3 | X-ray energy/frame-rate and AE passband were not specified in the available excerpt | Thin PBF specimen in the synchrotron beam; AE coupled through the solid specimen or substrate and synchronized with radiographs | Direct operando radiography, supported by post-process microstructure and solidification modelling | Directly confirmed that extensive cracking in unmodified CM247LC was primarily solidification cracking near the terminal stage of melt-pool solidification. Hf and nano-Y2O3 reduced cracking by different metallurgical/process mechanisms. This is compelling physical validation of AE timing, but synchrotron geometry is not representative of a normal bulk build and no detection/false-alarm rate was reported. (pqac-00000000) |
| Inline coherent imaging (ICI) correlated with synchrotron radiography | CM247LC, laser DED | Broadband low-coherence interferometry; 6 µm axial and 35 µm lateral resolution; 200 kHz measurement rate | Off-axis optical head at about 24° to the processing laser, with independently scanned and focused measurement beam | Simultaneous synchrotron X-ray radiography; ICI/X-ray surface-topology correlation greater than 0.93 | Resolved surface crack openings as small as 7 µm in valleys produced by track humping and related the surface signatures to subsurface crack growth or healing. It demonstrates direct optical detection when a crack opens at the surface, but the reported cracks were humping-induced in DED and are not automatically equivalent to every LPBF solidification crack. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000072, pqac-00000074) |
| Airborne acoustic sensing, including microphones, optical microphones and laser vibrometers | Reported mainly for laser DED; a SiC-particle-reinforced 316L example generated microcracking during rapid cooling | Distinct audible component around 12–16 kHz in the reinforced-316L example; conventional crack-related solid-borne AE is more commonly reported around 100–700 kHz, with peaks near 300–600 kHz | Contactless microphone or optical microphone within/near the process chamber; laser vibrometer aimed at the substrate or deposited component | Optical microscopy, liquid-penetrant inspection or other conventional inspection; cracked samples showed voids/surface defects while crack-free samples were smoother | Crack-associated bursts can be separated from process noise with high-pass filtering and time–frequency analysis. Evidence is largely for DED thermal-stress, layer or HAZ cracking rather than rigorously proven LPBF solidification cracking; gas flow, pumps, plume and laser modulation are major confounders, and robust false-alarm rates are generally absent. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005) |
| Thermography or pyrometry | Multiple LPBF/DED alloys; no aluminium hot-crack study in the available evidence directly imaged crack initiation thermally | Typical Si NIR: approximately 0.4–1.0 µm; InGaAs SWIR: approximately 0.95–1.7 µm; two-colour high-speed imaging examples used about 700 and 950 nm | Coaxial for the melt pool or off-axis for the track tail, heat-affected zone and layer-scale heat accumulation | Usually correlated with metallography, CT, process parameters or thermal models rather than direct crack-opening observation | Measures the causal environment—temperature field, thermal gradient, cooling rate, remelting and heat accumulation—not the crack itself. Two-colour Ti6Al4V imaging measured roughly 1–40 K/µs cooling and 5–20 K/µm gradients, but emissivity, plume attenuation, reflections and geometry can make temperature estimates misleading, particularly for aluminium. Treat it as a crack-susceptibility covariate unless independently validated. (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000055) |
| Visible layer or high-speed surface imaging | Potentially applicable to surface-breaking cracks in crack-prone Al and Ni alloys; no direct demonstration of LPBF hot-crack detection was established in the reviewed evidence | Visible/NIR bands depend on illumination and filters; detectability is governed principally by object-side sampling, contrast and crack opening | Off-axis through a protected chamber viewport; layer camera after exposure, or high-speed microscope viewing immediately behind the melt pool | Requires registration to metallography or CT; layer-anomaly studies instead validated features such as streaks, swelling, spatter and porosity | A sufficiently open surface crack can be visible, as the 7 µm ICI result shows, but ordinary layer images mainly reveal secondary manifestations such as dark lines, raised edges or changed reflectance. At 26 µm/pixel, the planned camera cannot reliably resolve typical micron-scale hot-crack openings; it may reveal larger connected or surface-breaking cracks over several pixels. No defensible detection or false-alarm rate for hot cracking is available. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028) |


*Table: Methods are separated into direct crack detections and indirect susceptibility measurements. The table highlights validation strength and the important absence of robust detection and false-alarm rates in most studies.*

**Structure-borne acoustic emission (AE)** is the most accessible laboratory method. Seleznev et al. coupled a broadband high-temperature D9215 piezoelectric sensor to the aluminium baseplate beneath LPBF-built Al₉₂Mn₆Ce₂ specimens using high-temperature grease, with 40 dB preamplification, a 50–600 kHz band-pass filter, and 2 MHz / 18-bit sampling (pqac-00000047). Crack-related waveforms were triangular bursts of 1–3 ms duration with spectra peaking near 100 kHz and extending to approximately 500 kHz (pqac-00000048). Validation against Zeiss Xradia Versa 510 micro-CT at 2.85 µm voxel size showed all four CT-identified crack locations in one build were associated with AE activity, but a triple-crack site produced only one detected event, possibly because the cracks occurred simultaneously or fell below the 90–100 dB threshold (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049). Crucially, a substantial proportion of crack signals occurred during the first five minutes after build initiation and also during post-build cooling, with crack formation potentially delayed by up to an hour after the responsible layer was built (pqac-00000051). No formal detection rate or false-alarm rate was reported, and the inert-gas circulation pump was a significant noise source requiring waveform-based discrimination (pqac-00000049).

**Regarding AE through a heated plate with thermal breaks:** The Seleznev study coupled the sensor directly to the aluminium baseplate through high-temperature grease, with the sensor described as "high-temperature" but with no stated operating temperature limit (pqac-00000047). For the described machine's ceramic thermal break and bolted/foil interfaces, one should expect significant ultrasonic attenuation and mode conversion at each interface. Practical approaches include: (a) coupling a waveguide rod directly to the build plate below the thermal break, bringing the signal to a sensor at a cooler location; (b) using a high-temperature sensor rated to ≥200–300 °C (the MISTRAS D9215 is rated to approximately 500 °C Curie temperature); and (c) establishing a pencil-lead-break transfer function for every plate/gasket/bolt configuration to verify that crack-frequency signals propagate with detectable amplitude.

**Operando synchrotron X-ray radiography** synchronized with AE on CM247LC confirmed that micro-cracking occurs during solidification, primarily at high-angle grain boundaries near the terminal solidification stage, and that both Hf and nano-Y₂O₃ additions mitigate cracking through distinct mechanisms (pqac-00000000). This approach provides definitive physical validation but requires beamline access and thin-specimen geometry unrepresentative of bulk builds.

**Inline coherent imaging (ICI)** detected surface crack openings as small as 7 µm in humped CM247LC DED tracks, with an off-axis head at 24° and <10 µm lateral registration accuracy. ICI surface-topology measurements correlated >0.93 with synchrotron radiography (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000072). Although demonstrated in DED rather than LPBF, ICI can in principle be integrated coaxially in LPBF systems.

**Airborne acoustic sensing** has captured 12–16 kHz audible signals from microcracking in SiC-reinforced 316L DED composites (pqac-00000001), but this evidence is from DED thermal-stress cracking rather than rigorously proven LPBF solidification cracking.

**Thermal sensing** does not detect the crack itself but monitors the causal thermal environment—gradients, cooling rates, and heat accumulation—and can serve as a cracking-susceptibility covariate (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034).

**Crack timing relative to the melt pool:** Solidification cracking occurs near the terminal stage of solidification when tensile stresses separate solute-rich interdendritic liquid (pqac-00000000). In the AE data, some cracks formed during the build (within seconds of lasing the responsible layer) while others were delayed by minutes to an hour during post-build cooling (pqac-00000051). The melt-pool tail in Ti6Al4V extends approximately 400–1000 µm behind the laser and solidifies in 200–600+ µs (pqac-00000057), suggesting that solidification cracks open within millimetres of the melt pool. Surface visibility depends on crack opening; ICI resolved 7 µm openings (pqac-00000003), but typical LPBF hot cracks in aluminium alloys may remain smaller and subsurface.

---

## 2. Coaxial Melt-Pool Sensing Through a Galvo Scanner

### Photodiodes vs. two-colour pyrometers vs. cameras

The planned single-channel silicon photodiode (520–985 nm, ≥100 kHz) is a proven baseline. Photodiodes offer fast response, high sensitivity and straightforward integration, with demonstrated sampling rates of 10–100+ kHz (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000045). However, a single broad-band channel conflates temperature, melt-pool area, emissivity and plume effects into one scalar signal.

**Two-colour (ratio) pyrometry** adds a second spectral channel and uses the intensity ratio to reduce emissivity dependence. A system by Hooper (2018) used two Photron FASTCAM SA5 cameras with ~700 nm and ~950 nm bandpass filters at up to 200,000 fps and 128×128 pixels on a Renishaw AM250, measuring Ti6Al4V melt-pool temperatures from approximately 1000 to 4000 K with cooling rates of 1–40 K/µs and thermal gradients of 5–20 K/µm (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056). Calibration used a stabilised tungsten-halogen source (Thorlabs SLS201L) illuminating an integrating sphere inside the build chamber, with radiance verified by a calibrated spectrometer; validation against a type-C thermocouple showed agreement within 1% while the laser was on and 5% at ~1900 K after shutoff (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054). A simpler two-InGaAs-photodiode pyrometer has been demonstrated at 1260 nm centre wavelength, 100 nm bandwidth, 1200–2900 K range, and 560 µm spot (pqac-00000008).

**For aluminium alloys**, two-colour pyrometry faces serious challenges. Aluminium has very low emissivity (~0.1–0.2 for liquid) that changes rapidly with oxide state, temperature and phase. A dual-pyrometer study on AlSi10Mg at 200 kHz detected melting modes but produced counterintuitive lower temperatures over shallow overhangs because the signal collapses melt-pool size, shape and temperature-profile information (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012). The low emissivity means weak thermal emission in the NIR, compounding signal-to-noise challenges.

### Effects of 1064 nm galvo mirror coatings and f-theta chromatic aberration

The basiCube 20 mirrors are coated for 1064 nm. Kozjek et al. (2026) note that galvanometer mirror coatings optimised for the working laser wavelength can strongly suppress other bands: a spectrometer test found that wavelengths in the 750–875 nm range were "almost completely blocked" by one scanner's mirror coating (pqac-00000064). Therefore, **before purchasing any coaxial sensor, the end-to-end spectral transmission through the actual basiCube mirrors and f-theta lens must be measured**—ideally with a broadband source and fibre spectrometer at multiple scan positions.

The f-theta lens is designed for 1064 nm; at other wavelengths, chromatic aberration produces wavelength-dependent focal shift and lateral image offset. Hooper noted that imaging at ~700 and ~950 nm through a 1064-nm-optimised scan head required independent camera-position adjustment for the two channels, and that galvanometer-dependent image offsets had to be mapped and corrected as a function of build-plate position and wavelength (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000066). The focal distance also varies with scan position in the build plane (pqac-00000065). A pre-focusing unit can partially compensate (pqac-00000063), but coaxial camera imaging through a basiCube without a camera port will likely be limited to low-resolution intensity collection rather than sharp spatial imaging of the melt pool.

**Practical recommendation for this machine:** Since the basiCube 20 has no camera port and the mirrors may severely attenuate visible/NIR, the most robust coaxial upgrade is a second photodiode channel at a wavelength that transmits adequately, creating a custom two-channel ratio monitor. Measure the actual mirror transmission first, then select two narrow bands that both pass, avoid 1070 nm, and fall within InGaAs or Si detector response (pqac-00000064, pqac-00000065).

---

## 3. Off-Axis High-Speed Imaging of Melt Pool and Spatter

Research LPBF testbeds have demonstrated a wide range of off-axis high-speed imaging configurations:

- **Ultrahigh-speed (1 Mfps):** Sakai et al. used a Shimadzu HPV-X2 at 1,000,000 fps with 200 ns shutter, 400×250 pixels, and a 20× Mitutoyo M-PLAN NIR infinity-corrected objective. Illumination was a Cavitar CAVILUX HF at 640 nm with a 60 ns pulse and four-direction beam splitting; a 645±10 nm bandpass filter was used. The illumination source was 23 cm from the sample (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000023).

- **LLNL testbed:** Calta et al. used an 810 nm pulsed laser (500 W peak, Cavitar) for coaxial illumination and high-speed X-ray + optical imaging (pqac-00000022 context from paper search results).

- **Off-axis thermal/visible cameras at moderate speed:** Thanki used a Mikrotron Eosens 3CL at 20,000 fps, 120×120 pixels, 100 µm/pixel, 30 µs exposure, 25° from vertical, with a 975 nm short-pass filter (pqac-00000019). Mitchell et al. used two cameras at 6500 fps, 65×80 pixels, 21 µm/pixel, with 750 nm and 900 nm filters (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000021). Lough et al. used off-axis IR at 2500 fps with a 1450 nm filter and 130 µm/pixel (pqac-00000017).

- **DED illuminated imaging:** An 808 nm illumination laser with 10 µs pulse and 810±10 nm bandpass filter was used at 100 fps/150 µs exposure, with the camera 320 mm from the nozzle at 30° (pqac-00000022).

**Window protection from condensate:** The 2-inch fused-silica window with a replaceable cover slide is essential. Metal condensate from aluminium alloys is aggressive; the cover slide should be replaced frequently. A gas curtain or laminar-flow screen across the viewing window helps. Steep viewing angles reduce condensate deposition.

**Cheapest useful setup:** An entry-level high-speed camera (Kron Chronos 2.1-HD at ~$5,000–7,000, capable of ~20 kfps at reduced resolution) paired with a used 808 or 850 nm CW diode illumination module (~$300–1,000) and a matched 10 nm bandpass filter (~$200), plus a long-working-distance zoom lens (Navitar 12× or similar, ~$1,500–3,000), can resolve melt-pool shape and gross spatter dynamics at 10–20 µm/pixel over a few-millimetre field. This would cost approximately $7,000–12,000 total. A Cavitar CAVILUX HF system (~$30,000–50,000+) is superior for pulsed illumination and freeze-frame quality but exceeds the stated budget.

---

## 4. Powder Spreading and Layer Quality

### Image resolution and lighting for defect detection

Scime et al. demonstrated that side-lighting and low camera angles produce high contrast, with 60–99% anomaly detection depending on defect type and machine; pre-recoat images target spatter and porosity, post-recoat images target swelling, incomplete spreading and recoater streaking (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028). Lu et al. used a Nikon DSLR with white LED illumination at 10–13 µm/pixel, achieving Pearson correlation up to 0.78 between pixel intensity and XCT-detected pores (pqac-00000024). An inline powder scanner at ~5 µm resolution detected powder unevenness, ultra-high edges and grooves (pqac-00000025).

The planned 12 MP camera at ~26 µm/pixel is adequate for streaks, short feed, raised edges and spatter deposits. It will not resolve individual 30–60 µm particles reliably. Adding two independently strobed raking-light directions and one diffuse top light, plus HDR/flat-field calibration, will maximise contrast.

### In-situ height mapping

**Fringe projection profilometry (FPP)** has been integrated into LPBF chambers. Zhang et al. (2016) achieved approximately 6.8 µm lateral sampling and 0.47 µm single-point height repeatability on a 28×15 mm field, resolving 28 µm peak-to-valley recoater waviness and detecting fused material protruding above the powder level (pqac-00000027). Practical in-machine vertical accuracy is more commonly ~10 µm; IN-718 builds measured part edges to within 100 µm laterally and surfaces to within 10 µm vertically (pqac-00000024). Multi-phase-shift FPP requires several images per measurement, limiting real-time capability but feasible for inter-layer inspection (pqac-00000030).

**Inline coherent imaging (ICI)** provides 7 µm axial resolution, 25–35 µm lateral resolution, and measurement rates from 50 kHz to 312 kHz (pqac-00000068, pqac-00000070). Single-point height repeatability is 0.30 µm over 100 seconds (pqac-00000068). ICI scans coaxially through the processing optics and has been used to detect raised regions, depressions, recoater-blade damage (striations in powder layers) and to perform closed-loop correction of surface roughness with a 54% reduction in maximum roughness (pqac-00000073). However, ICI integration requires coupling into the laser beam path, which is complex with the basiCube 20.

**Low-coherence scanning interferometry (LCSI)** at LLNL produced powder-bed height maps at 100 µm lateral spacing and 25 µm vertical resolution, sampling at 100 kHz (pqac-00000024).

**Recoater-mounted laser-line profilometry** (e.g., Keyence LJ-V7060) provides micron-level surface mapping over a 15 mm swath, detecting gouges, ridges and super-elevated features, though it did not report numerical accuracy (pqac-00000029).

**Imaging the spreading process itself** at high speed inside a chamber has not been convincingly demonstrated in the reviewed literature. Eschner et al. tracked individual powder particles with a two-camera stereoscopic system (pqac-00000026), but this assessed particle motion rather than the powder heap ahead of the blade.

---

## 5. Thermal Imaging in a Small Chamber

### Camera types and spectral ranges

Three spectral ranges are relevant, with distinct trade-offs:

- **NIR (Si detector, ~400–1000 nm):** Silicon sensors are limited to temperatures above ~700 K (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036). They offer high resolution and frame rates (up to 200,000 fps for scientific cameras) and use standard fused-silica or B270 glass windows, making them compatible with the existing chamber window. However, they cannot see the cooling track below red heat.

- **SWIR (InGaAs, ~0.9–1.7 µm):** More sensitive to cooler material, allowing observation of the cooling track tail and heat accumulation patterns. SWIR cameras are more compact and affordable than MWIR and are recommended as the practical choice for integration into small chambers (pqac-00000037). The existing fused-silica window transmits adequately to ~2 µm. Frame rates of 500+ fps with cropped ROI are typical. The melt pool may saturate; ND filters are needed (pqac-00000036).

- **MWIR (3–5 µm):** Best sensitivity to near-ambient and moderate temperatures and can capture full-layer thermal maps. However, fused silica is opaque at MWIR wavelengths—a sapphire, CaF₂ or ZnSe window would be required, adding cost and complexity. MWIR cameras are also more expensive. Altenburg et al. concluded that SWIR and MWIR provide more useful temporal and spatial temperature information than VIS cameras (pqac-00000037).

### Aluminium emissivity challenges

Emissivity of aluminium varies strongly with oxide state, temperature, wavelength, phase (powder vs. liquid vs. solid), and surface condition (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036). Liquid aluminium has very low emissivity (~0.1–0.2), producing weak thermal emission relative to steel or titanium at the same temperature. The result is that any single-wavelength thermal measurement is essentially a radiance measurement, not a temperature measurement, unless emissivity is independently known or controlled. Two-colour pyrometry reduces but does not eliminate this problem, particularly when the emissivity ratio varies with temperature (non-grey behaviour) (pqac-00000055). For aluminium LPBF, thermography should be treated as a tool for relative comparisons (track-to-track, layer-to-layer, region-to-region) and thermal trending, not for absolute temperature measurement.

### What thermography reveals

Thermal imaging has shown heat accumulation in overhangs and thin walls (slower cooling, longer melt-pool tails), geometry-dependent cooling rates, and thermal-gradient variation with scan strategy (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000057). It can identify locations likely susceptible to cracking by virtue of anomalous thermal history, but no reviewed study directly imaged crack formation thermally. In Ti6Al4V, Hooper measured cooling rates of 1–40 K/µs and thermal gradients of 5–20 K/µm, with overhang scans showing greatly reduced cooling and prolonged solidification (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000055).

---

## 6. Data and Synchronisation

### Signals to record

The NIST AMMT architecture provides a reference model. It records: commanded XY position and power (XYPT format, 10 µs between points), DAQ-measured galvanometer X/Y encoder feedback, laser modulation (gate), analog laser power (sampled at 25 kHz), coaxial melt-pool camera images with hardware triggers, layerwise images under multiple LED positions, oxygen sensor, and thermocouple readings (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000061). For the described machine, the full signal list should include: scan-controller XY commands and laser gate from the SCANLAB RTC interface, actual galvo encoder positions, commanded and measured laser power, coaxial photodiode(s), acoustic emission (raw waveform and/or parameterised hits), off-axis cameras (layer and high-speed), plate thermocouples, chamber O₂, dew point, pressure, and gas-flow proxy (anemometer or differential pressure).

### Synchronisation

A 500 µs digital synchronisation pulse triggered sensors in the NASA/NIST testbed, with camera exposure timing combined with the trigger to determine scan position (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000059). Exact temporal synchronisation between galvo-scanner commands and monitoring measurements is essential for high-resolution spatially resolved data; the SCANLAB RTC controller can output a position-synchronised trigger signal. At 100 kHz photodiode sampling and 1.1 m/s scan speed, samples are separated by ~11 µm along the scan path—commensurate with the melt-pool scale. Use hardware timestamps rather than PC arrival times.

### Data rates and storage

Kozjek et al. estimated that a typical PBF-LB/M build using one photodiode plus laser and galvo position data at 100 kHz generates tens of gigabytes (pqac-00000044). Adding raw AE waveforms at 2 MS/s and high-speed camera frames will increase this substantially; a small build might produce 50–200 GB, while extensive instrumentation on larger builds can exceed 1 TB.

### Standards and misleading data

The NIST AMMT datasets are publicly available from data.nist.gov and represent a de facto reference format using registered CSV files with per-layer, per-part structure (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000062). ASTM F3490 (AM data package) and ISO/ASTM 52942 (qualification) address data requirements at a higher level but do not prescribe signal-level schemas. Documented cases of misleading data include: (a) coaxial pyrometry on AlSi10Mg overhangs producing counterintuitive lower temperatures for hotter, narrower, deeper melt pools because the signal conflates geometry and temperature (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012); (b) emissivity-related errors in absolute temperature measurements (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000046); and (c) coaxial-only monitoring missing process signatures outside the melt pool (pqac-00000046).

---

*Table: Ranked additions for a small aluminium-alloy LPBF testbed, emphasizing crack-detection evidence, information gained per dollar, integration constraints and realistic budget ranges.*

### Rationale for the ranking

**Acoustic emission ranks first** because it is the only affordable sensor that has been demonstrated to detect crack initiation in-situ during LPBF of a crack-prone aluminium alloy, including delayed cracking during post-build cooling—information that no other sensor provides at any price (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000051). It is also inexpensive and minimally invasive.

**The second coaxial channel ranks second** because it upgrades the already-planned photodiode from an intensity monitor (sensitive to every confound) to a ratio measurement with reduced emissivity dependence, at modest cost (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012). However, the basiCube mirror coatings may limit wavelength choices and require careful spectral characterisation before purchase (pqac-00000064).

**Off-axis high-speed imaging ranks third** because it provides direct visual evidence of melt-pool shape, spatter, plume, denudation and potentially surface cracks—information essential for understanding aluminium LPBF phenomenology and correlating with the other scalar sensors (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000019). An entry-level system is achievable within the budget.

**The DAQ/synchronisation backbone ranks fourth** because without it, the other sensors produce interesting but unregistered data that cannot be correlated spatially or temporally with specific tracks, layers and defects (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000058).

A complete first-tier instrumentation package (AE system + second photodiode channel + entry-level high-speed camera + DAQ backbone + airborne microphone + layer camera lighting upgrades) can plausibly fit within $15,000–25,000, leaving headroom for a SWIR camera or fringe projection as a second-tier addition.

**Within a $20,000–40,000 total budget**, items 1–5 and 8 (the incremental layer-camera upgrade) can be achieved, with either item 6 (SWIR camera) or item 7 (fringe projection) depending on whether thermal mapping or height mapping is prioritised. For crack-prone aluminium alloy screening specifically, the SWIR camera is arguably more informative than fringe projection because it reveals cooling-rate and heat-accumulation anomalies that drive cracking susceptibility.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides relevant evidence mainly for in-situ crack monitoring in L-DED, but it does not specifically identify solidification (hot) cracking, LPBF, laser welding, acoustic-emission frequency bands, sensor placement, synchrotron X-ray methods, or the precise timing of crack formation relative to the melt pool. Acoustic emission (AE) was used to monitor layer cracking associated with thermal stress and HAZ cracking, and to monitor crack extension by relating AE amplitude and duration to crack location. In mixed-metal powder deposition, machine-learning methods, including K-Means clustering, distinguished pore-generated from crack-generated signals. A deep-learning SRCD model detected crack defects with 99.76% accuracy, while t-SNE-based time/frequency-domain processing achieved over 89% classification accuracy under different process parameters. AE is therefore presented as useful for real-time defect diagnosis, although weak signals, environmental noise, and high-temperature limitations complicate acquisition; contact sensors may require cooling. Thermal monitoring used contactless pyrometers and infrared cameras to capture melt-pool temperature and cooling behavior, but the excerpt does not report direct detection or temporal localization of hot cracks. Thermal methods are also limited by emissivity, reflections, plasma, and powder-flash interference. No synchrotron X-ray evidence is included.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not describe in-situ sensing methods, sensor types, frequency bands, sensor placement, or validation procedures for detecting solidification (hot) cracking during LPBF, laser welding, or DED. It does, however, provide relevant metallurgical context for interpreting such detection studies. During rapid solidification of nickel superalloys, local instabilities at the solidification front can produce primary and secondary dendrites. Low-solubility elements segregate into the liquid regions between dendrites, forming liquid films. These films are identified as common initiation sites for micro-cracks when internal stress exceeds local material strength. Complex alloys with wide solidification ranges are particularly vulnerable because they allow more time for liquid films and potentially deleterious phases, including Laves, tau, and carbides, to form. In LPBF, cellular microstructures generally dominate, and the cells may be treated as primary dendrite arms for estimating spacing and liquid-film stresses. contexts.context: The excerpt provides useful background for comparing coaxial melt-pool sensing technologies. It characterizes a pyrometer as effectively a single-pixel thermal camera, while noting that pyrometers may be mounted off-axis or coaxially. In a coaxial configuration, the sensor shares the laser’s optical path and requires a dichroic mirror whose transmission and reflectivity vary with wavelength; this is directly relevant to understanding how laser-wavelength coatings, including those near 1064 nm, can affect imaging and thermal detection. The excerpt does not provide specific 1064 nm mirror-coating data, f-theta chromatic-aberration analysis, or calibration procedures using blackbodies or tungsten lamps. It also does not compare photodiodes, two-colour pyrometers, and cameras in detail. Regarding wavelength selection, it states that vapour-plume radiation spans approximately 1–10 μm, substantially beyond the bands commonly filtered by L-PBF infrared monitors, and emphasizes that temperature estimation is difficult because the moving plume has complex, non-uniform emissivity. This emissivity issue is relevant to interpreting melt-pool temperatures, including for aluminium alloys, although aluminium-specific temperatures and emissivity values are absent. The excerpt’s strongest contribution is therefore the optical architecture and measurement limitations: coaxial alignment, wavelength-selective dichroic optics, high-rate pyrometry, and uncertainty caused by emissivity and spectral-band selection.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly compares several coaxial SLM melt-pool sensing approaches. A Concept Laser/KU Leuven system combines a high-speed NIR CMOS camera and a photodiode. A partially reflective mirror directs the 1064 nm laser toward the scanner while transmitting melt-pool radiation at 780–950 nm to the sensors; the incoming radiation can be integrated into a single melt-pool intensity value. The 1280 × 1024 CMOS camera also measures melt-pool shape, size, geometry, and temperature distribution, while both sensors can operate at 10 kHz, subject to the camera’s limited field of view. Other coaxial systems use a two-wavelength pyrometer connected by optical fiber, with two InGaAs photodiodes, a 1200–2900 K range, a 1260 nm central transmission wavelength, 100 nm bandwidth, and a 560 µm measurement diameter. CCD cameras measure brightness profiles, with reported sampling up to 20 kHz. The excerpt also discusses coaxial illumination and a pre-focusing unit designed to mitigate axial and lateral chromatic aberration from f-theta optics across different wavelengths. It does not provide calibration procedures using blackbodies or tungsten lamps, nor specific aluminium-alloy melt-pool temperatures or emissivity analysis.

contexts.context: The excerpt compares coaxial photodiode, pyrometric, and camera-based approaches for monitoring meltpool depth in PBF-LB/M, but it does not provide specific information about galvo scanners, wavelength bands, 1064 nm mirror-coating effects, f-theta chromatic aberration, blackbody or tungsten-lamp calibration, or aluminium-alloy meltpool temperatures and emissivity. It reports that simple photodiode-based coaxial measurements are generally unsuitable for reliable meltpool-depth control because their spatially integrated signals can contain high-frequency variations that do not represent actual depth changes. Two-color photodiode measurements demonstrated relative depth-change information only for AlSi10Mg, within a restricted process range and conduction-welding mode; absolute depth was not obtained, and constant laser power was required. Shielding-gas flow and non-Gaussian beam shapes may affect applicability. Camera-based systems preserve spatially resolved two-dimensional information about the meltpool and surroundings. A coaxial camera with a physics-based model achieved reported average depth-prediction errors of 2.8–9.9% for SS316L, though it was not tested across all scanning situations. Two-wavelength imaging pyrometry was reported for IN718, while single-channel pyrometry was studied on powder-free tungsten; both require broader validation.

contexts.context: The excerpt compares coaxial pyrometry and camera-based melt-pool monitoring, emphasizing the role of dichroic mirrors in separating laser and thermal radiation. A 316L study used a pyrometer behind a mirror reflecting 1070 nm while transmitting 1500–1700 nm; its 100 kHz measurements were spatially registered to the galvo position and strongly correlated with porosity. The passage highlights the temperature–emissivity circular dependency and identifies multi-wavelength detection as a way to address it, while warning that morphology can still cause misinterpretation. It also describes coaxial visible and infrared cameras: binary visible-light images of melt-pool size and shape predicted porosity with 78–93% accuracy, while an 850–1000 nm camera correlated overheating with swelling defects. contexts.context: The excerpt compares optical approaches for LPBF melt-pool monitoring, although it does not specifically discuss galvo-scanner optical paths, 1064 nm mirror coatings, f-theta chromatic aberration, tungsten-lamp calibration, or aluminium-alloy emissivity. Photodiodes provide fast response, high sensitivity, and straightforward integration; they have been used to measure melt-pool emissions, area, width, and length at sampling rates up to 10–20 kHz, while multispectral photodiode sensing reached 100 kHz. Their limitations include temperature-dependent characteristics and poor temperature stability. Two-colour pyrometry uses two InGaAs photodiodes for non-contact high-temperature measurement. Coaxial installation synchronizes the monitored area with the melt pool and is considered more suitable for real-time in-situ temperature measurement than stationary off-axis arrangements. However, pyrometry can be affected by dust and smoke and lacks spatial resolution. High-speed cameras measure melt-pool size and shape, with coaxial and off-axis configurations reported; X-ray imaging can reveal internal dynamics and pore formation. For thermography, an IR camera was calibrated against a reference blackbody up to 1050 °C, while another system was calibrated to 1700 °C. The passage provides no melt-pool temperature or emissivity data specifically for aluminium alloys.

contexts.context: The excerpt is directly relevant to coaxial melt-pool monitoring using two-colour thermography and high-speed cameras. A commercial Renishaw AM250 was modified to image melt-pool emissions coaxially with the laser path. This arrangement keeps the melt pool centered as the galvo scans, preserving spatial resolution over the build area. A dichroic beamsplitter transmits the laser wavelength while reflecting shorter-wavelength melt-pool emission into an imaging enclosure; a short-pass filter protects the cameras from laser reflections. Two Photron FASTCAM SA5 cameras, independently adjustable for differing focal lengths, recorded filtered radiation at approximately 700 and 950 nm, with up to 200,000 frames/s, 128 × 128 pixels, and 12-bit depth. Coaxial pyrometers share the laser optical path and require a dichroic mirror to reflect the laser wavelength while transmitting thermal radiation. In the cited 316L example, a 1070 nm laser was reflected and 1500–1700 nm radiation transmitted; the pyrometer sampled at 100 kHz and its approximately 635 μm spot covered the melt pool. Signal levels correlated strongly with porosity, with normalized values above 0.75 associated with a 95% pore probability, apparently distinguishing conduction, transition, and keyhole modes. Dual-wavelength pyrometry can address the intensity–temperature–emissivity problem, but melt-pool geometry can cause misleading temperatures: hotter, narrower, deeper pools at shallow AlSi10Mg overhangs were interpreted as cooler. Coaxial cameras provide melt-pool size and shape information that pyrometers lose. A visible camera using 450–900 nm radiation achieved 78–93% porosity prediction from binary images, while an 850–1000 nm camera correlated overheating with swelling defects. The excerpt therefore supports comparisons of coaxial pyrometry and imaging, wavelength selection, dichroic optics, and emissivity/geometry limitations, but provides no aluminium alloy absolute temperatures or calibration procedures.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports the use of inline coherent imaging (ICI) for in-situ monitoring of full 3D powder-bed-fusion layer morphology. ICI provides an immediate qualitative or morphology-based check of surface roughness, recoater-blade damage, powder packing density, protrusions, and depressions. Recoater damage can appear as striations in powder layers, while protrusions and depressions can be identified and manually corrected during a build using laser ablation and powder refilling. contexts.context: The excerpt provides general guidance relevant to thermal imaging in LPBF, but it does not identify particular LPBF camera models, viewing-window materials (sapphire, CaF2, ZnSe, or germanium), frame rates, or specific aluminum emissivity values. It emphasizes that thermal cameras are wavelength- and sensor-dependent rather than universally accurate. Silicon detectors cover approximately 400–1000 nm and are commonly restricted to near-infrared wavelengths above 800 nm because metals near their melting temperatures emit relatively little visible radiation. Silicon sensors are effectively limited to temperatures above about 700 K, while InGaAs sensors covering 950–1700 nm can detect cooler temperatures, potentially making them useful for observing cooling behavior; however, the melt pool may saturate such sensors. Neutral-density filters can adjust the measurable temperature range. Temperature calibration may use the Sakuma-Hattori equation, blackbody furnaces, and in-situ thermocouples, but assumptions of constant emissivity and blackbody behavior introduce substantial errors. The excerpt therefore supports interpreting thermography primarily as a tool for relative thermal signatures, cooling behavior, and process monitoring, while warning that quantitative cooling-rate or defect/crack conclusions require careful wavelength selection, calibration, and emissivity treatment. snippets: The mainstream sensors and in-situ data collection devices proposed in the literature can be grouped into the following major categories
i) non-contact temperature measurements (i.e., pyrometers and infrared (IR) imaging), ii) imaging in the visible range, iii) low-coherence interferometric imaging.

Reported acquisition rates include 10 kHz for a high-speed CMOS camera and photodiode, and 20 kHz for a CCD-camera/pyrometer arrangement. It also notes that coaxial monitoring may miss process signatures beyond the melt pool.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general information on acoustic-emission (AE) crack detection in metal additive manufacturing, but it does not identify or report the specific Seleznev LPBF study requested. It explains that sudden stress release during crack initiation generates transient elastic waves, which piezoelectric AE sensors convert into electrical signals. The waveforms can provide information about defect type, intensity, and spatial location. Crack-related emissions are described as short-duration, sharp-amplitude, high-energy signals, while process noise is generally more continuous and lower in amplitude. AE sensors may operate from tens of kilohertz to nearly 1 MHz; rapid crack initiation is associated with bursts around 300–600 kHz and above, whereas slower crack growth or instabilities produce lower-frequency components. Signal processing methods include STFT, CWT, time-domain analysis, high-pass filtering, HPSS, and bandpass filtering. Machine-learning methods reportedly distinguish cracks from porosity with detection accuracies up to 94%. contexts.context: The excerpt provides the study’s principal measurement results but does not specify the exact peak-temperature values beyond the captured measurement range, nor does it identify the material, detailed laser/process parameters, two-colour pyrometry calibration procedure, or the coaxial imaging arrangement through the Renishaw AM250 galvo scanner. Hooper reports that a two-wavelength high-speed imaging thermography method measured melt-pool surface temperatures approximately from 1000 to 4000 K at 100 kHz with 20 µm spatial resolution. The measured cooling rates ranged from 1 to 40 K/µs, while thermal gradients ranged from 5 to 20 K/µm. These values varied with process parameter, component geometry, and scan-path location. Scan-line starts and ends and hatch-direction turns made the melt pool more volatile and affected thermal gradients and cooling profiles. Overhang scans cooled significantly more slowly because the underlying unconsolidated powder had low thermal conductivity, despite reduced laser power. The method was validated against a type C thermocouple. Relevant measurement uncertainties include attenuation by the plume, wavelength-dependent attenuation, changing surface angle, unequal emissivity, and reflected radiation within the vapor-pressure depression, all of which can bias the inferred temperature ratio.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents the two-colour high-speed temperature-imaging calibration, validation, material, machine, and scan parameters, but it does not include the numerical peak melt-pool temperatures or cooling rates from the subsequent results. Calibration used a stabilised tungsten-halogen source (Thorlabs SLS201L) illuminating an integrating sphere inside the build chamber. A calibrated Thorlabs CCS200 spectrometer measured the sphere radiance, which was compared with each high-speed camera’s image intensity to determine the wavelength-dependent constants A1 and A2 in the two-colour-ratio equation. An aperture stop was used to reduce intensity and test camera linearity; Figure 5 relates intensity ratio I1/I2 to temperature. Validation employed a type-C tungsten-rhenium thermocouple in argon, heated by a 330 ms stationary laser pulse approximately 0.5 mm from the junction. Imaging agreed within 1% while the laser was on and remained within 5% at approximately 1900 K after shutoff, with increasing noise as the signal declined. The test material was Ti6Al4V, built on a Renishaw AM250 using a 1070 nm continuous-wave fibre laser focused to a 65 µm spot and power-modulated for point-by-point pulsing. Parameters were: hatching 170 W, 75 µm point distance, 60 µs exposure, 65 µm hatch spacing; inner border 170/75/60; outer border 85/45/40; and overhang 155/75/60/65. The excerpt does not provide the coaxial optical layout or galvo-scanner details beyond identifying the AM250.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the optical and calibration methodology for Hooper’s coaxial two-colour pyrometry system on a modified Renishaw AM250 LPBF machine, but it does not provide the measured peak temperatures, cooling rates, material, laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, layer thickness, or other process parameters requested. The coaxial arrangement used the machine’s scan head, F-theta lens, galvanometer mirrors, dichroic beamsplitters, relay/focusing optics, and two high-speed cameras. Optical transmission constraints led to bandpass filters centered at approximately 700 nm and 950 nm. Because the imaging wavelengths differed from the laser-design wavelength, galvanometer-dependent image offsets caused the melt pool to move within the image plane. The scan-head mirror-position feedback was recorded, and measured offsets were fitted as functions of build-plate x-y position and wavelength, allowing software registration before pixelwise intensity-ratio calculations. For two-colour temperature calibration, a stabilized tungsten-halogen source (Thorlabs SLS201L) illuminated an integrating sphere inside the build chamber. Its spectral radiance was measured with a calibrated Thorlabs CCS200 spectrometer and compared with each camera’s image intensity to determine the wavelength-dependent combined optical, filter, and detector efficiencies (A1 and A2).

contexts.context: The excerpt documents an AMMT-style in-situ monitoring architecture centered on synchronized melt-pool imaging and laser-power measurements. The optical setup uses dual cameras mounted coaxially with the laser, with approximately 5 µm/pixel spatial resolution. The left camera uses a 730 nm bandpass filter and a 333 µs exposure. Data acquisition includes camera and DAQ channels, an oxygen sensor, thermocouple, galvanometer position signals, laser modulation, and analog laser-power output. A 500 µs digital synchronization signal triggers the sensors. The recorded galvanometer X- and Y-position signals identify the scan-mirror locations, while image exposure timing is combined with the synchronization trigger to determine the nearest spatial image position. Laser control is represented by laser ON/OFF modulation, and the analog power output is sampled at 25 kHz. The monitoring system records laser-response timing and associates power measurements with position and time, enabling point-wise identification of response anomalies. Melt-pool imaging provides richer spatial data but is limited by emission-related sampling constraints, data-storage requirements, and complex interpretation. The excerpt does not identify photodiodes explicitly, nor does it specify documented data standards, file formats, metadata schemas, or certification standards.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a coaxial optical arrangement for melt-pool imaging, but it does not specifically quantify the effects of 1064 nm galvo-mirror coatings, f-theta chromatic aberration, focus shift, field distortion, or wavelength-dependent resolution. It does establish several relevant design considerations. A dichroic beamsplitter is inserted before the scan head so that laser-wavelength light passes through while shorter-wavelength melt-pool emissions are redirected into the imaging enclosure. This implies that the transmission/reflection behavior of components in the 1064 nm laser path is central to whether other wavelengths can be collected efficiently. The coaxial geometry keeps the melt pool centered as the laser scans, helping maintain spatial resolution across the build area, although no field-distortion measurements are reported. The two imaging channels use separate band-pass filters centered at 700 and 950 nm, and the cameras can be moved independently to compensate for different focal lengths at the two wavelengths; this is the paper’s direct treatment of wavelength-dependent focus rather than a quantified analysis of f-theta chromatic aberration or focus shift. The reported camera capability is up to 200,000 frames/s at 128 × 128 pixels and 12-bit depth, defining the stated detector-level resolution limit.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses how coaxial optical components can constrain imaging at wavelengths different from the laser wavelength. Machine optics are optimized for the working laser wavelength, so galvanometer mirror coatings may strongly suppress monitoring bands; a cited spectrometer test found that 750–875 nm wavelengths were almost completely blocked by the galvanometer scanning-mirror coating. Lenses, mirrors, and filters can also attenuate the selected meltpool-emission wavelengths, while their wavelength-dependent transmission/reflection must be considered when selecting camera bands. The text further notes that different optical-element incidence angles produce different transmitted/reflected intensities, making calibration dependent on the exact positions and orientations of the optics. Regarding coaxial-camera resolution, spatial resolution should be defined at the build plane in µm/pixel and selected relative to the smallest meltpool feature to be quantified. Coarser sampling can prevent meaningful recovery of meltpool shape, boundaries, and internal intensity or temperature gradients; increasing spatial resolution may reduce field of view and acquisition frequency. However, this excerpt does not explicitly discuss chromatic aberration of f-theta lenses, wavelength-dependent focus shift, or field distortion. It therefore supports the general optical-transmission and resolution aspects of the question, but not detailed conclusions about those specific lens aberrations.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses several optical issues in coaxial melt-pool monitoring. In the described SLM arrangement, a partially reflective mirror is designed to reflect the 1064 nm processing laser toward the scanner while transmitting melt-pool radiation at other wavelengths, specifically 780–950 nm, to the camera and photodiode. Thus, the mirror coating’s wavelength-dependent reflectance/transmittance is fundamental to separating laser light from emitted process radiation and enabling coaxial imaging. The excerpt also notes that f-theta lenses have different imaging properties at wavelengths other than the processing wavelength. This produces axial and lateral chromatic aberrations, which can cause wavelength-dependent focus shifts and image misregistration or distortion. A pre-focusing unit is introduced to compensate for these effects and ensure that the focal plane remains coincident across the wavelengths of interest. Regarding camera limitations, the cited system uses a 1280 × 1024 pixel NIR CMOS sensor, allowing melt-pool geometry and temperature-distribution measurements. However, achieving the stated 10 kHz sampling rate requires reducing the camera’s field of view to a limited region of interest, indicating a tradeoff between temporal sampling and spatial coverage. The stated depth/axial resolution is 6 µm, the transverse/lateral resolution is 35 µm, and the measurement rate is 200 kHz. ICI measures track-surface morphology and can capture surface roughness, sintered powder particles, waviness, and humping. Importantly, the study reports in situ recording of the morphology signature of crack openings at the track surface, while simultaneous synchrotron X-ray radiography was used to relate these surface signatures to subsurface cracking. The excerpt emphasizes robustness to high-power laser light and process emissions, and describes integrated scanning and focusing optics within the DED system. It does not provide a numerical layer-height measurement accuracy, nor does it explicitly state that the ICI optics are coaxial with the processing laser; it only establishes inline integration and optical integration into the process setup. Therefore, the excerpt supports resolution, acquisition-rate, morphology-monitoring, and surface-crack-detection capabilities, but does not establish LPBF-specific performance or a quantified layer-height accuracy.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an in situ fringe-projection surface-topography system for LPBF, not inline coherent imaging (ICI), so it does not provide ICI-specific specifications or a direct comparison. The reported lateral sampling is 6.8 μm/pixel, based on a 4160 × 2091 pixel camera and a 28 × 15 mm field of view. Height capability is assessed through phase repeatability: 30 phase maps of a flat powder layer produced a standard uncertainty of 0.00091 waves and a calculated single-point repeatability of 0.47 μm. The system acquires two measurements per layer—after powder spreading and after laser fusion—enabling assessment of powder-layer flatness, layer-height consistency, fused-region height, and process evolution. The measurements reveal grooves at fused boundaries, fused-versus-unfused height differences, splatter drops, waviness, and layer-dependent roughness. The excerpt suggests that surface markers may help detect defects such as pores, and that measured surface structures can support process control and yield assessment, but it does not establish crack-detection capability. It also does not report a measurement rate, layer-height accuracy as a validated absolute accuracy, or coaxial integration with the processing laser. The described system uses fringe projection with a 0.52 mm/cycle effective wavelength for the demonstrated measurement.
